The length of $B^0_s$ particles' life span was determined by analyzing the decay process $B^0_s \rightarrow K^+K^-$, taking into consideration various possible contributions from CP-violating phases and long-lived top-quark induced decays. The results showed that the typical value of the difference between the $B^0_s$ and $\bar{B}^0_s$ lifetimes' length is less than 0.2 picoseconds, with a standard deviation of 0.1 picoseconds. Additionally, it was found that the probability of the top-quark induced decays occurring at a specific rate is extremely low, around $10^{-5}$, and these decays would result in a slight difference in the forward-backward asymmetry of the $K^+$ and $K^-$ particles' decay angles.

This paper investigates the numerical solution of a control problem governed by a stochastic differential equation, specifically focusing on the control of a stochastic heat equation subject to a boundary control. The paper proposes a discrete approximation method using a Galerkin spatial discretization and a theta-scheme in time, and analyzes the convergence of the discrete solution relative to the control parameter. The analysis involves establishing the existence and uniqueness of the discrete solution, and converging the discrete solution to the continuous solution as the discretization error decreases.

New findings from the Pierre Auger Observatory reveal significant variations in the cosmic-ray flux above 4 EeV, with a detected feature size ranging from 69 to 332 meters in depth. Statistical analysis shows that the fluctuations in the cosmic-ray density in areas of 100 square meters of the observatory's surface correspond to a standard deviation of 0.061 +/- 0.009 in depth. Additionally, a more in-depth examination of the data revealed an average increase of 22 +/- 9 percent in the flux of cosmic rays within areas of 70 meters in depth around the most probable locations of extensive air showers created by the highest-energy cosmic rays identified by the observatory.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider's experimental facility in CERN has been utilized to analyze data from 2013's LHC run at a 5.02 TeV proton-proton energy of 866 nanobarns. Measurements obtained from the detector indicate a 0.5 TeV proton-proton energy and assess various aspects of charged particle spectra along with nuclear alteration factors in proton-proton and lead-proton collisions. Nuclear alteration factors are calculated based on a comparison of charged particle densities in proton-proton and lead-proton collisions at a 1.54 TeV nucleon-nucleon energy of 5.08 nanobarns. Measurements obtained from the detector indicate a 0.5 TeV proton-proton energy and assess nuclear alteration factors in the zero-zero rapidity range along with central rapidity semicircles.

This work presents an analysis of noncommutative quantum disks based on the su(1,1) Lie algebra. A key aspect of this investigation is the identification of two distinct parametric spaces associated with the commutator matrix, which arises from the algebra's defining properties. In order to gain insight into these parametric spaces, the study employs a transformation of the commutator matrix into a block diagonal form, facilitated through a unitary transformation derived from the algebra's unitary representation. A resulting antipodally symmetric quantum disk commutator matrix emerges from this transformation, and it demonstrates a self-reciprocal polynomial property. A further examination of this subalgebra reveals its relationship to the (1,1) Lie algebra, specifically in regards to the quantum disk's reflection and rotation symmetries. A discussion of the historical context of these algebras sets the stage for this investigation.

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training a deep learning model to categorize tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) from whole-slide images of lymph node sections. The task is crucial in understanding the relationship between TILs and patient outcomes, as well as in monitoring the progression of disease in response to treatment. To simulate a non-centralized data setting, we created a virtual FL platform comprising virtual agents contributing images along with corresponding labels. The results of our experiments using both the entire dataset and a more limited subset of participants showed that federated learning can effectively categorize TILs with high accuracy. Furthermore, our analysis indicated that the efficiency of FL can vary depending on the similarity between the datasets contributed by individual agents. To enhance the performance of FL in such scenarios, we developed a data preprocessing method that removes low-grade TILs from contributing images and removes the background from the evaluation images. The proposed method led to a significant improvement in the accuracy of FL, which was particularly notable in cases where the similarity between contributing datasets was low.

In this study, a key challenge in fiber-optic communications is identified: the decision-feedback equalizer is hampered by a high frequency-branch ratio requirement due to severe burst-error propagation in submarine fiber-optic transmissions. This requirement leads to an exponential increase in computational load, which cannot be met in 100G and 400G transmissions. To resolve this issue, a new frequency-domain equalizer design is proposed to suppress burst-error propagation. The effectiveness of this design is demonstrated in field trials, showing that it can significantly reduce the frequency-branch ratio requirement by approximately 90%. As a result, the increased load is minimized, enabling efficient transmission of 100G and 400G signals.

Temporal convolutional networks have gained popularity in various tasks due to their efficient use of memory. However, TCNs employ a sequential computation approach that can lead to performance bottlenecks when dealing with real-time applications. This issue is addressed by trimming unnecessary computations within a data batch, enabling parallel processing and reducing memory requirements. This approach is a non-linear optimization technique that leverages a network's future information to minimize unnecessary operations. We propose a simple and effective trimming in time (PIT) algorithm that can be easily integrated with existing memory-aware TCN implementations. Our experiments demonstrate that PIT leads to significant performance gains of up to 2.5 times with minimal accuracy drops of 1.5%. This is particularly evident in memory-constrained scenarios where reduced computation leads to reduced memory usage.

This paper aims to introduce a novel modification to the vector space $V$ over a given field $K$, along with a set of linear operators $f: V \times V \to V$. We've established a specific condition, dubbed the "strong condition", which ensures the uniqueness of a modified algebra structure, known as the Zinbiel algebra, on $V$. In this paper, we'll demonstrate that the Zinbiel algebra structure is characterized by the "strong condition" being met, which results in the algebra being abelian in nature.

Our research examined the behavior of flow fluctuations in 2.73 and 5.02 TeV Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. We analyzed the dependence of flow fluctuations on the transverse momentum threshold, $p_{\rm cen}$, and found that fluctuations in the flow of charged particles are unaffected by $p_{\rm cen}$ in a certain range. We also investigated the relationship between flow fluctuations and the impact parameter, and found that fluctuations in the flow of charged particles are higher in collisions with smaller cross sections, which is consistent with the idea that nucleon-level fluctuations contribute to initial conditions. We analyzed the behavior of flow fluctuations in different intervals of flow amplitude, and found that fluctuations in the flow of charged particles are lower in collisions with larger flow amplitudes. We also investigated the relationship between flow fluctuations and stream density, and found that fluctuations in the flow of charged particles are higher in collisions with lower stream densities, which is consistent with the idea that nucleon-level fluctuations contribute to initial conditions. We analyzed the behavior of flow fluctuations in different intervals of flow amplitude, and found that fluctuations in the flow of charged particles are lower in collisions with larger flow amplitudes. We also investigated the relationship between flow fluctuations and flow amplitude, and found that fluctuations in the flow of charged particles are lower in collisions with larger flow amplitudes. The uniform correspondence theory developed by R. Suszki has been the basis for numerous correspondences established between DLE-logic based frames and normal modal epistemic logic (NMLE) based Kripke models. These correspondences have enabled the transfer of proof techniques and the determination of semantic equivalences in the realm of NMLE. This paper builds upon existing correspondences by extending the correspondences to cover additional NMLE Kripke semantics, specifically including those defined by pre-openness, pre-closedness, and S5 semantics. Furthermore, this paper introduces a new framework that utilizes the concept of pre-frames, bridging the gap between DLE-logic based frames and Kripke models. This framework facilitates the identification of semantic equivalences in the realm of DLE-logic.

Informational discrepancies in data tables pose a significant problem, particularly when handling null values and functional dependencies. Existing research on structural differences focuses on empty cells caused by missing data and functional relationships. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework to address these complexities, incorporating null values and transitive dependencies within its model. It identifies a key issue in this domain, represented as a problem XAP (XML Anti-Peeling), which involves identifying all possible sub-trees in an XML document that contain no discrepancies. To solve this problem, the paper proposes a algorithm based on finite state machines, which can be optimized using a form of backward searching. The effectiveness of this approach is highlighted through an example dealing with data consistency in databases, and a theoretical comparison is made to demonstrate its superiority over a naive alternative. The proposed algorithm has been implemented and shows promising results in practice.

This research introduces a novel temporal varying parameters model, called Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregression (TPAR), to analyze and forecast count-based time series data sets. Unlike conventional specifications such as Poisson AR (PAR) and Negative Binomial AR (NBIAR), TPAR can accommodate and model temporal changes in the autoregressive parameters. A statistical framework for estimating the time-varying parameters was adapted from the switching regression approach, using which time series data can be forecasted. In addition, an asymptotic theory for the estimated parameters was developed, and a simulation study was conducted to assess the performance of the forecasts. Case studies using real-world datasets demonstrated the superiority of the TPAR model over traditional PAR and NBAR specifications.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), an object representation that uses
neural networks to encode object information in a manipulation task. This
representation uses the 3D coordinates of points relative to the object to focus
on its shape and orientation. To ensure 3D pose invariance, we use the equivariant
properties of multilinear neural network layers. For training, we use a point
cloud representation of the object's 3D pose and label it as we would a 2D image.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of this representation by achieving a high
success rate in grasping and manipulating objects in a simulation environment
and in real-world applications. Compared to traditional approaches using
convolutional neural networks, NDFs exhibit greater robustness in the presence of
noise and deformations.

The SiD calorimeter for the ILD, a future precision upgrade to the ILC, has been designed with a silicon sensor and a steel absorber. This design provides 0 degree coverage and is made up of eight layers in the central section. Studies have shown that the number of layers can be reduced to six while still meeting the precision requirements for the ILD. This reduction in layers will allow for a smaller overall size, which in turn enables the placement of the forward pixel tracker within the forward calorimeter. This design change also enables the use of a single silicon sensor type for both the central and forward sections, which simplifies the design. Additionally, the silicon sensor thickness can be increased to 300 microns in the forward section to compensate for the lower energy in this area, which can also accommodate a 0 degree layer within the forward section. This design can provide 0 degree coverage and has been shown to meet the SiD photon identification performance requirements.

This paper delves into the analysis of a binary system composed of a subgiant star and a white dwarf, located in the Milky Way's bulge, discovered within the CAPOS field. We undertook a close examination of the star's past evolution. Our main findings are as follows: The white dwarf's mass is accurately determined as 0.64 ± 0.02 M⊙ through its cooling path. By modeling the system in its current and past states, we estimate the core mass of the subgiant to be 0.49 ± 0.01 M⊙. We also estimate the age of the system to be around 10.5 billion years, aligning with the H-rebranching of the core. We anticipate the subgiant to become a helium white dwarf in approximately 10 billion years. Notably, this system represents one of the oldest found in the CAPOS sample to date.

The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs contains over 800 theorem-proving developments across various disciplines, making significant contributions to software reliability through verification and validation. Despite the value it holds, the archive lacks a unified framework to guide users through its extensive collection of proofs. To address this limitation, our research involves analyzing the archive's underlying theorem-proving frameworks and identifying areas for improvement in the Isabelle proof assistant. We have developed a set of proposals to enhance the archive's readability and maintainability, ensuring the proofs remain compatible with the latest version of Isabelle. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these proposals, we created a revised version of the verification4isabelle framework, which showcases improved documentation, standardized naming conventions, and a more efficient verification process. Our research findings can be applied to other large-scale proof repositories, and our enhanced framework serves as a model for future developments within the archive.

Using the functional renormalization group at a next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity on the critical line for O(N) universality classes. We have confirmed that the singularity's universal position follows the $t^{\ast} \propto 1/N$ behavior for $N$ greater than two, providing a clear explanation for the singular ground state near the critical point in universality classes two through five.

In statistical mechanics, TAP's analytical approach introduced an optimized free energy function subject to constraints, and we analytically examined its properties. We found that under specific conditions, this constrained optimal free energy is locally concave, which is in line with the assumptions made in the Fernique-Zaidi analysis using the stochastic Langevin dynamics. Furthermore, we derived an explicit condition for the local concavity of the constrained optimal free energy. This condition can also be applied to generate a simplified proof of local concavity within the post-AMP framework.

Modern metasurfaces, at the intersection of advanced technology and science, 
constitute an intricate field that requires a thorough understanding of multiple 
areas, including electromagnetic theory, mathematical modeling, and engineering. 
Recent breakthroughs in this field, particularly those surrounding flat optics and 
manipulation of light, have left many researchers in awe. In the realm of physics, 
theoretical models have been developed to describe fundamental aspects of these 
phenomena, yet a comprehensive theoretical framework remains elusive. This paper 
attempts to bridge this knowledge gap by using a holistic approach that 
simultaneously leverages numerical simulation and analytical methods to investigate
metasurfaces. In the course of this research, we designed a generalized type of 
metasurface, numerically simulated its behavior using a high-frequency simulator, 
and subsequently verified our findings with a more general theoretical model. 
Our research provides a clear and concise framework for understanding the basic 
properties of any metasurface, paving the way for its application in various 
devices and systems.

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for smooth fully integrable vector fields near a specific point, $p$. Fully integrable vector fields have the distinctive property of being linked to gradient fields on their equilibrium points. However, this property does not extend to neighborhoods of those points. The key claim of this research is that every fully integrable vector field can be transformed into a linear vector field on a neighborhood of $p$ through a smooth change of coordinates. In order to prove this claim, the smooth local orbital linearization theorem is first proved, and then the field is put into a specific diagonal form with a particular change of coordinates before being fully linearized using a second change of coordinates. The key lemma of this research relies on the application of a formal orbital linearization theorem to a series expansion of the vector field near $p$.

This paper suggests a new approach to modeling the behavior of electrons within atoms and molecules using a limited set of variational parameters. These parameters represent the coefficients of Slater determinants, which are linear combinations of the actual wave function and are derived from a comprehensive configuration interaction calculation. In essence, our method views the actual wave function as a combination of a limited set of wave functions that are themselves made up of linear combinations of several Slater matrices. We utilized the Entanglement Partitioning Technique to determine an optimal configuration basis set and compared our results to established reference data for the helium isoelectronic series with a focus on ground states and by also incorporating neural network training without a reference energy value in mind. Notably, our deep learning model achieved an accuracy of 0.01 kcal/mol in predicting potential energy curves, outperforming even the most advanced conventional methods while also successfully identifying saddle points and local minima along the potential energy curves as demonstrated by calculations of dipole moments, ionization potentials, and correlation energies.

A striking alignment of high-energy blazars, named the Giant Structure, spans
approximately 1.5 billion light-years across the sky. Within this vast region,
there exists a massive curved arc of blazars on the sky, formed by 130
extragalactic objects. Using the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we have analyzed the
distribution of blazars in this region and found that their two-dimensional
projection on the sky does not match the expected curve if it were based on
distance from the center. Instead, there is a discrepancy of about 300
million light-years. We have also examined the relationship between this alignment and a group of
high-energy blazars known as the Cactus configuration, discovering that the
Giant Structure includes all four blazars in this group and that this shared
supervoid is located at the center of the Giant Structure. We have calculated
the mass of this supervoid and found it to be a massive $4.8\pm1.5\times10^{14}M_{\odot}$. Using this information, we have estimated the free fall time for this
group of blazars and found it to be on the order of 1 billion years. We have
also examined the distribution of blazars in this region and found that they
follow a two-dimensional projection of a triaxial ellipsoid with a major axis of
