In the context of automorphic forms, a key strategy involves using series expansions, specifically Eisenstein series, to develop relationships between different spaces of forms. These series typically have non-trivial zeros, and by analyzing their zero locations, researchers can establish connections between the spaces. The goal of this project is to explore the isomorphism between two spaces, $S_k(\Phi)$ and $S_k(\tilde{\Phi})$, for $k$ greater than or equal to $4$. Here, the spaces are defined using specific sets of polynomials, $\Phi$ and $\tilde{\Phi}$, and modifying them by groups that cancel discrete orbits. The challenge lies in handling the complex interplay between the combinatorial discrete mathematics of these orbits and the analytic properties of the Eisenstein series.

This study proposes a biophysical brain model for Parkinson's disease, utilizing computational neuroscience techniques and data from marmoset primate brains. The model is an advancement of the existing Fino framework, specifically designed to simulate striatal dysfunction in Parkinson's disease. It integrates experimental data on the effects of dopamine and levodopa to enhance realism, and includes detailed representations of dopaminergic neurons, the striatum, and their interconnected pathways. The model has the ability to produce complex neural dynamics, including both regular and irregular activity patterns, and has been optimized for levodopa's ability to treat Parkinson's disease through a process known as phase-locking. Furthermore, it incorporates an innovative method for identifying critical brain regions involved in the model's neural networks. To validate the model, we analyzed its neural connectivity and identified key network characteristics, including a mesoscale network structure and a large-scale network that is highly interconnected, and performed a series of computational experiments that mimic previous studies on levodopa's effects, resulting in outcomes consistent with those observed.

This research proposes an efficient anti-aliasing rendering technique for line junctions in vector maps, enabling a significant reduction in rendering times and a noticeable enhancement in visual aesthetics. The suggested method employs a basic geometric concept to determine overlapping areas along lines' intersection points, and then applies a standard 2D rendering technique to the resulting shapes for a more realistic effect. The proposed technique has been implemented and tested in a real-world rendering engine, demonstrating its effectiveness in both performance improvement and visual enhancement. The proposed technique has been found to achieve a 25% improvement in frames per second (FPS) in line junction rendering, and a 10% improvement in overall rendering FPS. The suggested method has also been found to provide a 10% improvement in user satisfaction in terms of visual aesthetics. The proposed technique has been found to provide a 10% improvement in user satisfaction in terms of visual aesthetics.

We present initial data obtained by the Koto Ultra-Optical Low-Resolution Low-Surface-brightness Spectrograph Integral Field Unit on the Seimei Telescope, centered on 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies observed at redshifts less than 0.04. Our observations with a 20 kpc$^2$ field of view gathered spatially resolved information on the galaxies' emission lines, including [O II] $\lambda$ 3727, H$\alpha$ $\lambda$ 6563, H$\beta$ $\lambda$ 4861, and [O I] $\lambda$ 6300, as well as continuum spectra, from 3703 to 7050 $\rm \AA$. Our data were collected over three to five on-source exposures lasting 2 to 3 hours each, and were reduced using the standard IFU reduction pipeline for the Seimei Telescope. These reductions yielded integrated spectra for 9 galaxies as well as 7 to 9 spatial slices for the galaxy pair F185604a-b, and we discuss the spectral analysis of these data, including any limitations imposed by our observations, in this paper.

This study proposes a new family of multivariate transcendental interpolation functions derived from the logarithmic form of the widely used thin plate spline (TPS) radial basis function. The proposed interpolation functions maintain the same form as the TPS, ensuring numerical stability and ease of implementation. A new set of radial basis functions is formulated, followed by the development of a quasi-interpolation operator that preserves the original function values and derivatives up to a specified order. The convergence analysis of the constructed operator is performed, demonstrating that it converges to the underlying function at a rate of O(h^p), where p is the order of the operator. Notably, this type of quasi-interpolation operator has not been previously reported in the literature. Numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the accuracy of the proposed operator in comparison to the traditional interpolation method based on the TPS.

Cloudy conditions within driving environments pose a significant challenge, as they can lead to reduced visibility and impair road safety. Automating the detection of severe weather conditions through rearview cameras has become a pressing concern for the automotive industry. This paper introduces a novel multi-class dataset, WeatherDB, comprising categorizations of four weather states (fog, rain, snow, and clear conditions) and undertakes data enhancement techniques to counter over-reliance on visual appearance. A comprehensive evaluation of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) is conducted to assess their effectiveness in weather identification. Our findings reveal that CNN performs exceptionally well on datasets with similar visual characteristics but struggle with diverse data sets, and that data augmentation has a limited impact on the accuracy of these models.

Separating speech from overlapping talkers in background noise is a complex task, especially when there are multiple loudspeakers, a phenomenon known as concurrent speech. This problem can be addressed as a signal processing task, specifically source separation, using techniques such as deep learning methods. Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of deep learning methods, particularly convolutional recurrent networks, in extracting clean target speech from mixed audio containing concurrent speech. This paper presents a novel dual-path CRCN architecture, in which two separate networks process different frequency ranges independently before their outputs are combined. The frequency ranges are divided into two distinct groups, and the combined output is fed into a shared recurrent unit. This architecture was evaluated using the Interspeech 2020 MUSAN dataset and was compared to a single-path CRCN architecture, and the results showed that the dual-path CRCN architecture achieved a higher permutation invariant loss (PIL) score with a lower mean squared error (MSE) than the single-path CRCN architecture.

A well-established problem in cosmology is the discrepancy between the observed distribution of galaxy rotation curves and predictions based on the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. We investigated the effects of heavy neutrinos and $f(R)$ gravity on the turn-around radii of dark matter halos using numerical simulations. In a flat $f(R)$ gravity model, we found that the turn-around radii of halos are increased by a factor of two to three due to the impact on neutrino free-streaming length. Introducing heavy neutrinos with masses between the electroweak and TeV scales resulted in a significant increase in the turn-around radii of small-mass halos, with a relationship that can be described by a power law. When combining these two factors, we found that the increase in the turn-around radii of small-mass halos can be explained by the standard $\Lambda$CDM model with a fifth force range on the order of 50 Mpc, which is consistent with the neutrino free-streaming length being influenced by the fifth force.

This research aims to explore the potential benefits and challenges of adopting a two-fluid model in studying atmospheric convection. Atmospheric convection is a complex, self-organizing process with distinct, interconnected scales, similar to those found in turbulent Rayleigh-Benard convection. Within this analogy, the onset of convection occurs when a critical temperature difference is surpassed, following which multiple convection rolls form and interact. However, implementing a two-fluid model in this context is a difficult task due to the extensive dynamic and thermal interactions between the two fluids. Our study employs a simple two-fluid simulation model, in which the model's 'atmosphere' (warm fluid) is separated from its 'ground' (cool fluid), to simulate this convergence. The model's 'atmosphere' undergoes significant convective mixing, resulting in average ground temperatures that are a mere 0.5 K from the desired mean temperature of the system, in contrast to a single-fluid model that struggles with non-uniform ground temperatures. Furthermore, the model's 'atmosphere' exhibits a more accurate temperature distribution across the system, matching the Benard cell temperature profile, than the single-fluid model. The model's 'atmosphere' also shows improved mass flux fluctuations when compared to the single-fluid model, using a two-fluid model with a high Schmidt number. The model's 'atmosphere' exhibits increased thermal fluctuations and a more accurate temperature difference across the Benard cell when using a low Schmidt number.

This paper suggests a method to genuinely entangle uncorrelated particles by emulating the Jaynes-Cummings interaction. Initially, two remote and independent quantum systems, represented by particles A and B, remain unconnected. To entangle them, particle A undergoes the JC transformation with a linear optical component that affects the environmental photon field represented by particle B. Measuring the output field allows researchers to retrieve the entangled state of particle B. Selectively manipulating the JC interaction with respect to the mode of the optical field creates a variety of entangling operations. Our proposal includes a pathway for the optical field to interact with the quantum systems of either ion species trapped within an optical cavity or superposed spin states of atoms pre they are prepared in separate cavities.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment's upgrade to the Large Hadron Collider's (LHC) upgraded detector will require a pixel detector with enhanced performance, particularly in tracking and fluctuation control. Although the upgraded detector's two-layer pixel system, operating at a 1.5 mm pixel pitch with a 3.2 GeV beta cut, outperforms the previous version in many areas, some issues persist. One such problem lies in the large gap between the two layers, which results in a significant "edge" region in the reconstructed tracks. To address this challenge, a new reconstruction method has been developed, and the results of its implementation in the "pilot" region of the CMS detector during LHC Run 2 are presented here. The new approach reduces the hit distance between the two layers' hits along the "edge" track and therefore significantly reduces the noise. When tested with Run 2 data, this method demonstrated a 25% improvement in the "pilot" hit efficiency within the "edge" region.

This study presents the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral function of the scalar SU(2) glueball within the framework of a finite temperature SU(2) gauge theory, using the lattice autocorrelation function method. A thorough investigation of the spectral function has been carried out to identify the SU(2) glueball at various temperatures, from just above the glueball's onset temperature to a temperature just low enough for the spectral function's characteristics to be clearly defined. The analysis focuses on how the spectral function changes with temperature, particularly its onset temperature, peak temperature, and width. It also compares the results to a zero-temperature SU(3) glueball calculation, finding notable differences in their mass parameters.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated a dataset of tweets to evaluate the
sentiment using an LSTM classifier. The annotation served as input to the classifier,
which used word embeddings to determine the sentiment. The annotated dataset and the
sentiment prediction model are available for download. We compared the performance of
the basic LSTM model to multiple enhanced models, including those using different
word representations, multiple LSTM layers, and a combination of LSTM and CNN.

A nonlinear interaction between gravitational and electromagnetic fields affects
the thermodynamic characteristics of an asymptotically AdS spacetime. Specifically,
we examine a family of non-linear charged AdS black holes and show that their
thermodynamic properties behave differently when the interaction between gravity and
electromagnetism is present. This is illustrated by calculating the heat capacity
and entropy spectrum of these black holes for both linear and non-linear interactions.
When the non-linear interaction is present, the heat capacity becomes negative in
certain regimes, indicating a phase transition between stable and unstable black
holes. This transition is further analyzed and found to result in the formation of
a shadow ring around the primary image of the black hole. This shadow feature
depends on the non-linear interaction parameter and distinct shadow patterns can
occur for different values of this parameter. The shape of the shadow ring can
be explained by examining the circular photon orbit surrounding the black hole.
This orbit, which gives rise to the shadow ring, is present only in the presence
of a non-linear interaction between gravity and electromagnetism.

We investigate the connection between the Wigner function's positive definite feature and its associated symbol representation, specifically how they relate to the generation of nonclassical entanglement and synchronization in multimode systems. Our analysis reveals that a positive definite Wigner function ensures the nonnegativity of the symbol representation, implying classical behavior. Nonnegativity of the symbol representation, however, does not guarantee positive definiteness of the Wigner function. We propose a measure for characterizing the deviation of nonpositive regions within the Wigner function and demonstrate its application to observe the onset of entanglement and synchronization in both two-qubit and continuous-variable systems.

Conversational interfaces are becoming increasingly prevalent, offering a user-friendly
alternative to interacting with computer systems. Given the complexity of establishing
a dedicated role for each user within these systems, a role-based framework would
significantly enhance their functionality. This paper presents a role-based framework
for open-domain conversations in English, incorporating a comprehensive user
identification system, a role assignment framework, and a set of predefined roles
suitable for one-on-one conversations. Our implementation leverages large language
models, integrating a user profiler, role classifier, and conversation manager to
facilitate seamless role-based conversations. We have evaluated our system in a live
setting, incorporating a dataset of over 10,000 user inputs to adapt to
unforeseen user behaviors. Our results show that our system effectively navigates
conversations within assigned roles, even in the presence of user errors or
ambiguity.

Precision agriculture's key component is the analysis of factors influencing crop health, and one effective method for this is through the use of statistical models, specifically generalized linear mixed models. In this research, a novel methodology for evaluating crop health metrics was developed, utilizing a strong spatial-temporal model to assess the structure of data and an information criterion to determine the most suitable model parameters. This approach was applied to a case study of strawberry disease management, and the results showed that the method successfully identified the most suitable model and extracted valuable information about the data. However, the study's findings were hampered by the large data set, and further analysis was limited to a smaller data subset. The research was conducted in collaboration with University of California Davis and the University of California Cooperative Extension, and the data used were obtained from the University of California Davis.

360-degree (Eulerian) 360-degree travel videos allow viewers to explore a scene
from any angle, providing an immersive experience. Current automatic prediction
techniques are limited to two-dimensional screens and lack methods to forecast
user views within the third dimension. This study proposes an original task
called 360-degree Caption-based Viewport Forecasting and develops a matching
approach using a 360-degree maskable version of the vision transformer. In
evaluating this concept, our research includes two rounds of human subject
studies to assess its validity and reliability. In order to prepare data for
these experiments, a 360-degree annotation framework is also presented along
with a 360-degree dataset called 360CF-Data. The proposed framework and
dataset are designed to facilitate research on 360-degree Caption-based Viewport
Forecasting.

Tensor network representations can illustrate the structure of diverse quantum states, 
including thermal states and the evolution of systems over time. This paper introduces a 
new type of tensor network, called the double-line tensor network, which accurately captures 
the thermal correlations present in classical nonequilibrium scenarios. It also effectively 
represents the temporal evolution of a system by transforming the initial state's tensor 
network into a new representation that reflects changes in the system's behavior over time. 
To apply this method, we can utilize a new variational algorithm that uses two tensor 
representations for the same quantum state, allowing us to obtain a precise tensor network 
representation of the thermal state or the temporal evolution of a system by analyzing 
its unitary propagation.

A critical challenge in modeling multi-component systems with cross-reactions involves controlling the complexity of the problem. The paper introduces a new method for modeling these systems, based on a scale-oriented approach that restricts reaction rates to specific ranges. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a simplified model of air quality, and then analyze its performance in the original model with cross-reactions. The analysis reveals that the method results in a condition of functional decoupling, allowing the system to be solved using independent numerical methods. The paper also explores alternative versions of the method, including one that uses a more direct approach to restrict reaction rates. The authors find that the most effective method results in a more complex algebraic condition than the original problem, but this condition can be simplified to obtain a decoupling condition similar to the direct approach method. The paper presents a case study of nitrogen dioxide emissions in the Los Angeles Basin, and discusses the implications of the method for modeling multi-component systems with cross-reactions. The authors propose that this method can be used to model general multi-component systems with cross-reactions by modifying the model to account for reactions that occur within specific ranges of concentrations. The paper also discusses the potential for this method to be used in conjunction with other modeling techniques, such as the quasi-equilibrium approximation.

In this research, we establish a precise inequality relating the nonisotropic mean curvature of a surface in the Euclidean space and its distance from a line. This inequality is used to create a new concept, the nonisotropic p-capacity, which can be viewed as a variation of the classical p-capacity where the surface's mean curvature is defined by a nonisotropic mean curvature operator.

The Microscope space test for the equivalence principle in the gravitational and metric sectors involves measuring the differential acceleration of two test masses as they orbit around the Earth. Microscope's mission relies on a sophisticated scientific apparatus comprising two test masses, a sensor unit, a data acquisition unit, and a light unit used for thermal control and data transmission. However, during the experiment, the data transmission is interrupted by glitches that occur when the unit switches from reception to transmission mode. These glitches result in the loss of scientific data and need to be addressed to ensure the success of the mission. The statistics of such glitches, which have occurred in previous missions, are analyzed along with potential strategies to mitigate their impact and reduce data losses during the Microscope mission.

The Activity Gradient Theory stands out as a simplified model that effectively
captures the complex behavior of colloidal particles interacting dynamically,
especially when the activity of particles near the surface is significantly
different from those in the bulk. This study delves into the unknown aspects of
this model by examining how it handles particles that change shape in response
to their surroundings. This dynamic behavior causes the activity of particles to
vary, leading to an interesting phenomenon known as mechanical hysteresis. Our
results reveal that this model predicts that particles that change shape will
move more freely in response to increased activity, which may result in them
getting trapped in narrow channels due to their altered dimensions. This study
also highlights the potential to improve the model by taking into account how
particles that change shape are affected by surface forces.

The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of k-hops covers required to cover all vertices in G. This paper examines the minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops for specific graphs, including trees, weighted trees, series-parallel graphs, and certain types of planar graphs. Specifically, we investigate the minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops for these graphs and provide upper and lower bounds for the number of covers needed. We also examine the k-hops strong nearest neighbor cover for these graphs and provide upper and lower bounds, along with specific cover configurations. These studies contribute to our understanding of cover-based search algorithms, which assign a cover to each graph vertex.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how this variance affects the interpretation of data from experiments at the Large Hadron Collider and future studies at a future collider, such as the Future Circular Electron-Positron Collider. Specifically, incorporating the variance according to its perturbative expansion, taking into account the impact of infrared renormalons, is being examined for its effect on predictions of differential cross-section data related to hadron production in deep-inelastic scattering processes. A mathematical framework for the color dipole gluon distribution's variance, given in terms of a perturbative expansion in the form of a Borel-Padé summation method, is being used to investigate the impact of infrared renormalons. This framework is being applied to estimate the variance's impact on predictions of cross-section data, given in terms of moments, such as the second moment, which can be compared to experimental results and theoretical calculations based on the Borel-Padé method. A key aspect of this analysis is the understanding of how the variance's impact is influenced by the choice of the cutoff parameter, often denoted as $\beta$, which characterizes the small-$x$ behavior in the saturation regime.

As the number of frogs increases, the frog model on a finite tree evolves into a stationary process. Researchers have previously established that, below a certain critical frog density, the model exhibits an abrupt shift from high to low activity levels. This critical density is believed to represent the point at which the model transitions from an activated state to a dormant one. In the frog model, the dormant state is characterized by a single, slowly moving frog that eventually comes to rest on a specific tree branch. This branch, which the frog initially starts on, is chosen at random based on the initial distribution of frogs. The frog's movement is determined by a random walk that is biased towards staying on the tree, and as a result, the frog's position becomes concentrated on a particular subtree with a specific density. This dense subtree, which the frog is likely to be situated within, has a density that is directly related to the frog model's equilibrium behavior. In particular, the density of this subtree is equal to the critical frog density required for the model to transition out of its dormant state. In the case of the one-dimensional line, this critical density was found to be one-third, and it remains unclear whether it remains the same in the context of the frog model on a tree.

Researchers have a long-standing interest in materials that respond differently to left and right circularly polarized light, known as chiral non-reciprocity. Achieving this property requires specific symmetry breaking techniques. This study introduces a novel approach, using a unique magnetophotonic surface lattice under normal light incidence. The lattice's design incorporates spatial symmetry breaking and an internal magnetic field, which together produce extraordinary optical properties, including non-reciprocity, negative differential conductivity, and a giant Faraday rotation. Importing this structure into a microcavity enhances these effects and generates circularly polarized light for approximately twice the typical time periods. Additionally, simulations demonstrate the potential of these structures to create non-reciprocal light-beam transmission, a Faraday filter, and an increased spontaneous emission in photonic cavities.

In recent years, numerous significant classification models have been trained on vast datasets, allowing them to efficiently classify a wide range of categories. However, these models are not always accessible due to intellectual property concerns or the need for extensive training data. In such cases, it may be necessary to leverage the knowledge of these models without revealing their underlying workings. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that enables the knowledge transfer of a black-box model, allowing a replacement model to perform equally well without training. In our experiments, we successfully demonstrated zero-shot knowledge transfer between black-box models by comparing the classification decisions of the original model against a threshold, effectively condensing its knowledge into a binary format that can be utilized by the replacement model. This method allows the replacement model to achieve comparable performance to the original model on unseen data by optimizing the decision-making process, rather than the classification process itself. Our results show that this approach is effective, achieving a significant improvement of up to 12% in accuracy on unseen classes in the Caltech-256 dataset and 2% improvement in the CIFAR-100 dataset, with only a single example of each class.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time,
using data collected by the LHCb experiment during the proton-proton collisions
at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Additionally, they have obtained the first
evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode. Both observed and
evidenced decay modes were discovered by searching for final states with a $K^0_L$
particle and a $D$ or $D^*$ system, where the $D^*$ signal was separated from the
$B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \gamma$ background by exploiting the $D^*$ decay to $D^0 \gamma$
and subsequent $D^0$ to three charged particles. Furthermore, they calculated the
branching fractions for both $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$
decay modes, along with the fraction of $B^0_s$ decays going to the $D^*$
instead of $D$.

Determining the complete lattice of submodules of a given module is a fundamental problem with far-reaching implications, especially in the context of commutative and computational algebra. Although various techniques can isolate certain submodules, as seen in the application to systems of polynomial equations, there are instances where even a single submodule cannot be found using traditional methods. In this paper, we introduce an original approach to constructing the lattice of submodules, starting from partial information. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness by generating the entire lattice of submodules for a given module more efficiently than existing strategies. Furthermore, we apply our approach to solve a system of polynomial equations, showcasing its potential to outperform current methods for finding all submodules of a given module.

Strong geodetic sets are a specific type of set that contains at least half of the total number of elements, plus one, within a particular distance from a central point. Given a strong geodetic set defined by a distance $d$, identifying its center can be achieved through a variety of algorithms. However, the challenge arises when the center is unknown, and only the set's members themselves are aware of their own inclusion in the strong geodetic set. Under this scenario, the problem is to determine the time it would take for the center to locate itself. This paper explores this scenario for both halfspaces and polytopes.

We have developed a novel approach to mimicry learning, which enables a student model to closely resemble an ensemble of highly accurate, but imperfect and varied teacher models, despite the student being constrained by limited and poor-quality data. In traditional supervised learning, the student is trained to match a single ideal target distribution representing the truth. In contrast, we have formulated a new optimization problem that allows the student to minimize the difference with a dynamic mixture of target distributions, representing the varied outputs of the teacher models. To solve this problem, we have designed an efficient TRAIL algorithm that uses an adaptive sampling strategy to selectively choose a diverse set of target distributions that best capture the characteristics of the ensemble, and used a combination of over-sampling and anti-sampling techniques to balance the mix of data. To evaluate our approach, we conducted a comprehensive study of TRAIL on the tasks of text classification and sentiment analysis, and demonstrated that it outperforms a strong baseline method that uses a fixed ensemble. Notably, TRAIL achieved a remarkable 95% improvement in accuracy on a sentiment analysis dataset with only 1% of the original data.

Intelligent assistants like Google Assistant and Siri must balance providing helpful information with avoiding overloading the user. Currently, machine learning models rely on explicit feedback from experts to adjust their performance, but this approach has several limitations. The proposed framework of one-shot multi-way observation learning addresses these challenges by allowing the models to adapt to different user observations without requiring expert input. The framework is tested on a dataset collected from real-world interactions between users and the Google Assistant, involving multiple observation categories. The results show that the proposed method can effectively learn from a single example to predict new instances of the same observation category, outperforming a baseline model by a significant margin. The study also highlights the importance of modeling sequential data and suggests that a first-order Conjugate Gradient algorithm can be an efficient solution for solving the system of linear equations. The proposed framework is a key step towards reducing the data needed for training and improving the overall performance of the models.

This paper calculates the error rate of a specific type of code called polar coding, particularly adapted for parallel access in PAC protocols, and contrasts this with the commonly applied density evolution calculation method. The discrepancy arises due to an inaccurate initial assumption about the code's performance when the binary free distance is 0.5, which needs to be adjusted through actual data calculation. The proposed correction involves determining the error rate from the polarization stream itself. The code's overall error rate performance is then calculated by combining the polar encoder with an optimum source code, using the maximum likelihood criterion, and the resulting calculation method differs from the conventional density evolution approach, leading to improved code performance gains reported in this paper.

Neural Machine Translation is a series of actions that involve selecting words to translate a phrase from one language to another. While it's typically modeled as a sequence-to-sequence problem, the extensive nature of possible actions makes it challenging to translate certain phrases, such as the phrases found in sentence summaries. In these situations, it's common to use abstractive Summarization models, which are often trained using a different approach than Machine Translation models. However, both models share a key characteristic: they are part of a series of actions that build on each other to ultimately produce a final translation or summary. Given this shared structure, it's possible to learn both translation and summarization skills in a single, unified framework. In this paper, we propose a new approach to learning Machine Translation in a data-driven way by breaking it down into a series of smaller action-learning tasks that build on each other. We then apply this approach to a Summarization task by treating it as a series of Machine Translation actions, and found that it outperforms the standard sequence-to-sequence baseline on the arXiv SummArivation dataset.

This paper presents a novel approach that leverages machine learning to enable a robot to determine its position and orientation in a camera's field of view, as well as estimate the location of its end-effector, without the use of markers, based on images captured from a single RGBD camera. A deep learning-based model is designed to predict these values in a simulated environment, which is then validated in a real-world setting using a Rebinocla RB5 robot equipped with an Intel RealSense D435i camera. Adjusting the robot's configuration to match the predicted positions involves an optimization process using a non-linear solver, with the solution verified through successful execution. Successful predictions and adjustments were achieved in a variety of scenarios, including those with limited field of view and occlusions, and the paper discusses the effectiveness of a range of hyperparameters, including resolution, input images, and optimization methods.

This study introduces the concept of a quasi-fractional skin area (QFS-area) that incorporates non-integral alpha-blending techniques in digital composition. By drawing upon parallels to traditional fractional flow theory, researchers can utilize QFS-area to analyze the behavior of alpha-blending regions within images. A fundamental characteristic of QFS-area is the identification of a critical point, where a significant change in its dynamics occurs. Furthermore, the relationship between a quasi-fractional skin factor and QFS-area has been established, allowing the latter to be calculated through the former's alpha-blending equivalent. A notable aspect of the study involves the application of a quasi-fractional skin factor to artistic creations, providing an intriguing example of the intersection of art and science.

The internet's growing influence on political discourse is reflected in changes in online behavior, particularly in how people consume news. This study analyzes 2 years of browsing history from 1 million Europeans, focusing on how users read online news in eight languages. It has been observed that users with liberal and conservative viewpoints have different online news consumption patterns. Although language barriers seem to have little effect on online news consumption, users' political divisions are reflected in the websites they frequently visit. It can be inferred that online news consumption reinforces users' existing conservative or liberal views.

We examine the word complexity of the R. Thompson group V, addressing a long-standing open question by investigating various aspects of its polynomial-like behavior. Our analysis shows that V's word complexity function grows in accordance with a quadratic rate, yet fails to meet the standard requirement of having a strictly positive coefficient. We also demonstrate that V's word complexity is responsive to changes in its generators, specifically displaying an increase in complexity when switching from the standard generators to their negations. Furthermore, we establish that the increased complexity of V's word complexity function resulting from its polynomial-like nature is inherently persistent, even in cases where other, more transient forms of complexity vanish.

This report outlines a comprehensive characterization of a quantum bit that has been consistently driven by a periodic torque. We have determined the long-term, steady-state properties of the system in question. We have also verified that the standard approach used to describe continuous driven systems in equilibrium is not applicable. Instead, we have developed an analytical method for predicting their non-equilibrium behavior. This method allows us to connect the steady-state properties of the system to its underlying periodic dynamics. We have validated our theoretical approach using an experimental quantum simulation based on a system of two atomic spins. We have observed that the system's non-equilibrium behavior can be understood in terms of its equilibrium counterparts at effectively modified chemical potentials. We have also observed that periodic driving can lead to a steady-state current in an otherwise isolated system. This phenomenon arises due to an imbalance created by the driving process. It cannot occur in equilibrium systems, as driven systems always converge to a steady state where the average values are the same as the initial values.

We explore how the biharmonic operators on hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space in higher dimensions are affected by repeated application of certain operators, ultimately establishing a framework for classifying these hypersurfaces as minimal or nonminimal. Our findings indicate that if a hypersurface undergoes the same operator twice (e.g., subject to the delta-operator twice), its harmonicity is maintained. In contrast, if the hypersurface undergoes different operators (e.g., subject to the delta-operator followed by the Beltrami-operator), its biharmonicity will be impaired. Our research also extends to hypersurfaces developed from repeated application of the Ricci-flow in the Euclidean space, enabling the classification of these hypersurfaces based on their biharmonic status.

A continued fraction expansion can be expressed using the formula: $x=[0;a_1,a_2,...,a_n,...]=\frac{1}{a_1+\frac{1}{a_2+\frac{1}{a_3+...}}}$
where $a_n$ represents a sequence of natural numbers with no finite endpoint, 
identifiable over $\frac{p}{q}$ means that there exists a fraction $\frac{p}{q}$, 
where $0<\frac{p}{q}< x$, and for all $n\geq 1$, we have $a_n\neq 1$ except for $a_1=1$. 
In this paper, we investigate the properties of identifiable continued fractions under $\frac{p}{q}$.

The axion's meager presence of evidence forces it to occupy a vast parameter space, 
which in turn demands that the "Shadow Substances" category, to which axions belong, 
be redefined in terms of the neutrino sector's "Shortfall". This redefinition, 
occurring at the "New Physics Threshold", can be as meager as $10^{-6}$ when 
considering the "Electroweak Era". As a result, the "Shadow Substances" category 
now encompasses not only sub-TeV, multi-GeV particles but also includes both 
"Heavier-than-axion" and "Lighter-than-axion" candidates. This reevaluation 
fosters a more comprehensive understanding of the "Shadow Substances" framework, 
which can be seen as a fundamental extension of the Lepton Flavour Theory.

China's first large sky survey spectroscopic telescope, LAMOST, operated from 2011 to 2018 and gathered a vast amount of data during its 3.5 years of full-capacity science observations. LAMOST's time-domain exploration capabilities allowed it to identify variable stars across its 4 $K$2 plates. A team of astronomers conducted an in-depth analysis of these data, discovering a wide range of variable stars including delta Scuti, beta Cephe, and slow pulsating variables, as well as rotational modulation, eclipsing binaries, and long-period variables. To verify the accuracy of their results, the team cross-referenced LAMOST's data with more than 1000 light curves obtained from the ASAS-SN catalog. They identified a significant number of variable stars including 12 delta Scuti stars, 5 beta Cephe variables, 2 rotational modulation variables, 1 beta CMa variable, 1 rotational modulation binary, 1 CW Leonis-type variable, 1 gamma Doradus variable, 1 rotational modulation semi-detached binary, 1 rotational modulation contact binary, 1 rotational modulation W UMa-type binary, 1 rotational modulation beta Per-type variable, 1 rotational modulation delta Scuti-type variable, 1 rotational modulation FK Com-type variable, 1 rotational modulation RS CV-type variable, 1 rotational modulation delta Del-type variable, 1 rotational modulation lambda Bootis-type variable, 1 rotational modulation

In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edge and texture information are intertwined in medical images, current deep learning approaches often inadvertently suppress the crucial edge information present in these images. To address this limitation, we propose an edge-based gated convolutional neural network (EG-CNN) that selectively prioritizes edge information within these images. The proposed network's unique feature is a convolutional neural network that acts as an image filter, allowing only edge information to pass through to subsequent texture extraction pathways. Through the application of EG-CNN to brain tumor segmentation, our experiments demonstrate the network's capacity to effectively capture the essential edge information necessary for accurate semantic segmentation. Compared to the baseline CNN, the proposed EG-CNN framework achieves comparable performance while outperforming models that solely focus on edge or texture information.

This research focuses on transactional validation for MongoDB, specifically
transactions implemented using the MongoDB driver for Java. MongoDB's
documentation outlines the requirements for atomicity, consistency, isolation,
and durability (ACID) in transactions. However, the MongoDB community has raised
concerns regarding the effectiveness of MongoDB's transaction implementation,
particularly in ensuring data consistency. To address these worries, this study
develops a validation framework for MongoDB transactions. The framework leverages
the test-driven development approach and utilizes JavaUnit tests to validate the
implementation of MongoDB transactions. Furthermore, the research employs the
validation framework to evaluate the transactional capabilities of MongoDB in
comparison to traditional relational databases featuring built-in transaction support.

We examine the chromatic symmetric polynomials of a directed acyclic graph in detail, focusing on their representation as a sum of monomials and the associated coefficients. Our analysis reveals that the coefficients of these monomials are non-negative when compared to a specific baseline, and this characteristic holds true for all possible combinations of the graph's nodes. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the monomials comprising the chromatic symmetric polynomials and an inverse matrix within the Kostka-Foulkes matrix, demonstrating that the entries of the inverse matrix comply with a specific pattern. This relationship enables us to deduce the non-negative coefficients of the monomials with a specific baseline, and as a result, we can infer the $e$-positivity of the chromatic symmetric polynomials.

The perception of a detection network is a critical component that lays the foundation for subsequent processing layers. Revising perceptions is a common technique used to enhance the performance of detectors by interpolating and moving the initial perceptions towards the labels associated with the bounding boxes, and numerous strategies have been proposed to this end. This paper introduces a novel approach to revising perceptions, centered on a contrastive loss function, and demonstrates that simply analyzing the relationship between the perceptions and labels after the delivery of outputs can serve as an effective means of revising them. Building on this concept, the authors developed a framework to reevaluate perceptions via hindsight summation, and evaluated its performance by revising perceptions across four detection networks on five datasets, achieving superior results compared to existing methods.

Deep learning models, particularly those based on convolutional neural networks (CNN), have excelled in interpreting and processing medical image data with minimal reference to explicit feature extractors. However, research has revealed the presence of innate biases within these models that are evident in their ability to classify medical images along various dimensions, such as gender and age. In an effort to thoroughly examine the extent of this phenomenon, a dataset of facial images was created across a broad spectrum of ages and in both male and female subjects. Subsequent analysis using this dataset revealed that the pre-trained models were capable of accurately distinguishing between male and female images, but struggled to accomplish this task when using the data that had not been pre-labelled. Furthermore, research indicated that the age range of these models was limited to the age they were trained on, with an inability to classify images outside of this range, despite having access to a broader range of images during training. In contrast, the findings showed that models trained on open-source medical datasets developed an age-based bias that was not reflected in the actual data, with an inability to distinguish between images of individuals under the age of 18 and those over 18. In addition, the research demonstrated that the use of multiple models to classify images led to an increase in accuracy over using a single model, with an average improvement of 6.5%.

In the field of complex systems research, there is a growing interest in studying networks that are not directly observable, but rather inferred from data sets that describe the interactions between components, the "concealed geometry" of these systems. In this research, we investigate nanoassemblies made of iron phthalocyanine molecules on a copper surface, where the assemblies molar energy release during a spin reversal can be measured in triads that interact in three different ways - once positively, once negatively, and with no effect. By comparing these energy releases, we identify the assemblies that switch spins and track their molar energy releases over time in three states, before, during, and after the spin reversal. During this spin reversal, the assemblies' energy releases show a significant increase followed by a decrease, and we find that this is a general phenomenon, regardless of the initial interactions between the triads. In some cases, the energy releases become synchronized over time, and we find that this occurs when the triads' interactions are positive, but only if the assemblies' switching points are synchronized. In the end, the triads' energy releases become desynchronized as the spin reversal is completed, and we find that this occurs when the assemblies' switching points are not synchronized. In addition, we find that the energy releases are more likely to become synchronized when the triads' interactions are positive, but only if the assemblies' switching points are synchronized. The solar wind plays a crucial role in the energy flow between the Sun and other planets. Understanding this energy transfer is key to comprehending how magnetic fields are generated in the solar wind. Observations made by the Parker Solar Probe between 35 to 109 million kilometers from the Sun's surface reveal the relationship between the solar wind's speed, density, and temperature. At these close distances, tiny variations in the solar wind's behavior become visible. Analyzing these patterns, scientists have identified two distinct periods of rapid solar wind variations: one that lasts around 400 seconds and another that lasts around 160 seconds. The amplitude of these variations increases as the distance decreases, reaching up to 0.25 times the speed of light. However, the variations' intensity remains the same regardless of the angle from the solar wind's direction. This discovery has significant implications for the way scientists study the solar wind and could potentially be used to study other similar plasma environments.

Speech emotion recognition, a crucial technology, has far-reaching applications, 
notably in customer service assessment, where it can personalise and improve 
interactions. Notwithstanding significant advancements in other areas of 
multimodal analysis, SER development is hindered by a substantial gap between 
training and testing conditions. This study introduces a novel approach 
to adapt deep reinforcement learning to real-world speech emotion recognition 
tasks across domains. Initially, a simulated training environment is created 
using a labeled dataset to teach a policy network to select optimal classification 
models, thus learning a transferable strategy. Next, this learned strategy 
is employed to select models that excel in the target domain, thereby sidestepping 
the issue of domain disparity. To enhance generalisability, a multi-task 
reinforcement learning framework is implemented, allowing the policy network 
to explore multiple classification models in the test domain. Experimental 
results indicate that this approach yields superior performance compared 
to conventional domain adaptation techniques and surpasses human accuracy 
in the FER+ dataset and the IEMOCAP corpus.

Understanding the behavior of magnetic materials under high-pressure conditions is crucial to uncovering their fundamental properties and potential applications. In this study, Aurivillius Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ was investigated under high-pressure and temperature conditions using a combination of magnetic susceptibility, X-ray diffraction, and nuclear forward scattering techniques. Initially, a high-pressure induced magnetic ordering above 1GPa was confirmed, along with a structural phase transition at 1.5GPa. Further investigation revealed a complex relationship between magnetic ordering, structural phase transitions, and chemical pressure, which was probed by varying the amount of oxygen in the Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15-x}$N$_x$ series under ambient pressure conditions. These findings suggest that Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ could be an ideal test bed for the interplay between chemical and external pressure effects within the A$_2$B$_2$O$_5$ type materials.

Previous methods for calculating the shortest path in discrete-continuous domains have been analyzed, and a general error estimation framework has been established. This framework is particularly useful in modeling real-world paths, as specified in the context of a free flight path optimization problem. In this problem, the goal is to minimize flight time between two points in a spatial region, subject to air traffic control constraints, which can be represented as discrete obstacles. The Reeds-Shepp controller is an optimal solution method, but its computational complexity makes it impractical for large-scale problems. As a result, a discrete shortest path is approximated using the A* algorithm, but this approach introduces errors in the calculation. The proposed error estimation framework can be used to bound the discrepancy between the approximate discrete path and the optimal continuous path. This bounding error can inform routing decisions, such as determining whether the A* algorithm should be relaxed to allow for grid transversals. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through a simulation of a free flight path optimization problem.

Researchers have previously discovered that the universe's expansion accelerates due to an unknown force, which they call "dark energy." One possible explanation for this phenomenon is the presence of a highly pressurized gas filling the universe. A new model has been developed to simulate how a highly pressurized gas expands within an infinite, empty space. However, this model has a flaw, as it includes an imperfectly evacuated region at the center. To correct this, a new model has been created to simulate the expansion of a highly pressurized gas within an infinite, empty space that has a spherical cavity. This model includes a type of shockwave that forms as the universe expands, and it shows that the energy of this shockwave remains constant over time, which is affected by the energy of the universe's expansion, the pressure of the gas, and the radius of the cavity. This model also predicts that the temperature of any objects located within the cavity will increase as the universe expands, due to the expansion of the universe itself. Additionally, this model provides a possible explanation for the high temperatures observed in some regions of the universe, such as the cosmic microwave background, and it suggests that these regions could be the result of shockwaves caused by the universe's expansion.

This paper determines the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate formula, taking into consideration $D_s^{*-}$ meson spin effects. The chosen form will be useful for extracting the $bs$ quark sector's form factors from experimental data, specifically those related to $|V_{cb}|$. The chosen form will be tested using the Belle experiment's $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate data to obtain the form factors $f_+$(w) and $f_0$(w) for the $D_s^{*-}$ longitudinal polarization.

A recent study by Gesztesy and Tsiganov linked linear Schrödinger operators and Lax representations on the real line has significant implications. This research extends the findings to a broad class of Lax pairs generated by Lax representations associated with the Toda field theory. These extensions lead to the creation of a wide range of Lax pairs derived from generalized Toda field theories. One key subset of these generalized Toda field theories can be linked to generalized Hermite polynomials. As a result, these generalized Hermite polynomials will serve as names for an even broader range of Lax pairs.

A unique phenomenon is reported where an adhesive tape, when unwound, generates a distinct sound pattern that transitions from random events to a synchronized, rhythmic occurrence. This shift is linked to the evolution of the tape's unwound structure, which changes from a disordered to a ordered form. As the tape unwinds, its surface develops a series of parallel creases, ultimately resulting in a rolled-up sheet with a periodic pattern of creases. The sound pattern is closely tied to the crease structure and is influenced by the speed at which the tape is unwound. A critical unwinding speed exists below which the sound remains irregular, above which a rhythmic pattern emerges. Adjusting this speed can switch the tape's sound output between these two states. The crease structure formed during unwinding is critical to the rhythmic sound phenomenon, which raises intriguing questions about the potential for more complex patterns to emerge in other systems that exhibit similar phase transitions.

Our analysis examines the complex phase behavior in planar Josephson junctions, specifically in SQUIDs with asymmetric loops. We find that in these devices, a 2D phase diagram accurately represents the dynamics, allowing for the identification of distinct regime lines that indicate a shift from stable rotation to unstable motion. The phase diagram's construction serves as a comprehensive tool for analyzing and predicting phase patterns, including both regular and irregular patterns resulting from magnetic flux variations. Our study demonstrates that in the regime of airgap modulation, phase dynamics in SQUIDs exhibit chaotic behavior, characterized by irregular rotation and possible phase slip events. The possibility of controlling phase slip events presents an opportunity for utilizing SQUIDs in the study of nonlinear phenomena.

Our analysis introduces a non-abelian modification to the ether term within the thermal bath, effectively describing the thermal fluctuations of the non-abelian "ether" within the universe. We then examine the implications of this modification on non-abelian gauge boson and Higgs fields at finite temperatures, considering both real and imaginary chemical potential. By doing so, we derive the thermodynamic potential, non-abelian charge, and non-abelian expectation values of these fields. We specifically investigate the impact of a non-abelian "ether" on the phase transitions of non-abelian gauge boson and Higgs fields, including both symmetric and non-symmetric cases, and we examine the stability of the vacuum by analyzing the Coleman-Callan effective potential. We also explore the influence of a non-abelian "ether" on the distribution of non-abelian gauge boson and Higgs particles within non-abelian "ether" and non-abelian "ether" within non-abelian gauge boson and Higgs fields.

This research introduces a novel approach to analyzing option collateral costs, taking into consideration both interest rates and hedging expenses. A dynamic hedging model is employed, requiring the posting of collateral, which incurs both interest and hedging costs. These costs are viewed as payments akin to fees, with specific strike-dependent characteristics. As a result, options can be viewed as derivatives based on the underlying asset's price, with specific payoffs at expiration. With this perspective, the time-value-of-money aspect can be separated from the option's intrinsic value, which is then determined by integrating the delta-hedged asset's price over a probability space. This integration yields a probability distribution of the option's payoff at expiration, which can be used to calculate its present value. This value represents the option's worth in the present, taking into consideration both interest rates and hedging costs. A numerical example is provided to illustrate the application of this approach to a specific scenario.

This research focuses on the long-term behavior of a variety of materials, 
specifically addressing their periodic and high-contrast variations. The main 
approach involves transforming the original material into a new one with 
differing properties, followed by an analysis of the original material's behavior 
within a specific time frame. The goal is to understand how a particular 
Gaussian measure affects the average characteristics of the material over time. 
The study focuses on two types of material variations: those with distinct 
orientations and those with distinct spatial locations. For the former, the 
analysis explores the effects of curved surfaces on the material's behavior, 
while for the latter, the study examines the impact of spatial location on the 
material's anisotropy.

Early-type galaxies experienced tidal features due to galaxy mergers. These features, however, fade over time, making them difficult to detect beyond 1 billion years. Using the Subaru Hyper Suprassai Sky Survey, we analyzed large early-type galaxies at 0.7 billion to 2.8 billion years in the Abell 2390 Supergalaxy Field and in the Phoenix Cluster. We identified tidal features within these galaxies and calculated their flux proportions. We found a lower flux proportion in galaxies with brighter central regions, especially those with 1.5 less stellar mass than the expected ratio. We also discovered a lower flux proportion in galaxies with higher specific stellar masses, likely due to major mergers disturbing these galaxies and making tidal features harder to detect. We found no correlation between flux proportions and times since the merger, but we did see a lower flux proportion in galaxies with higher specific stellar masses in the Phoenix Cluster. We estimated the merger rates in these clusters and found rates of 1.5 to 3.5 major mergers and 10 to 20 minor mergers per early-type galaxy at 1.5 billion years in the Abell 2390 Supergalaxy Field and 2 to 4 major mergers and 10 to 20 minor mergers per early-type galaxy at 1.5 billion years in the Phoenix Cluster.

A social dynamics model analyzes the long-term effects of social mobility across generations, allowing individuals to move up in status relative to those above them. The number of opportunities available in each status determines the rate of advancement. Varying the distribution of opportunities across statuses alters the social hierarchy's dynamics. The model reveals that narrow distributions of high opportunities in the lower statuses lead to stable, long-term distributions consistent with those observed in many real-world societies. In contrast, broader distributions of opportunities trigger a self-reinforcing cycle of concentration. The model also demonstrates that the key factor driving these outcomes is the relative advantage that individuals with more opportunities have in securing further opportunities, a phenomenon dubbed the "advantage of advantage". The model includes a quantitative analysis of the US birth cohort of 1955, showing that the distribution of opportunities in the lower statuses is relatively narrow, and the data supporting this includes the observed distributions of opportunities within each status. The model also highlights the potential for small changes in the distribution of opportunities to have significant effects on social mobility across generations.

The development of advanced laser systems necessitates a deep understanding of amplitude and phase distribution within their output field. While traditional methods for measuring this distribution are effective, they can be time-consuming and require extensive system disassembly for the collection of data. In contrast, a technique known as electrical field measurement enables the simultaneous measurement of both amplitude and phase distribution, with minimal disruption to the system. This method involves injecting a well-characterized electromagnetic wave into one port of a network analyzer, which then calculates the complex S-parameter of the device under test. In the context of a high-power laser system, we employed this method to measure the S-parameter of a device with a wide bandwidth, overcoming initial limitations. Through further optimization, we successfully measured the amplitude and phase distribution of the device's output field, with improvements including a more accurate measurement of the device's main lobe width, reduced side lobe levels, and verification of its symmetrical distribution.

We maintain an $\ell_p$ space with a specific dimension $n$, in which no substantial portion is contained within a particular subspace of lower dimension. Our goal is to verify that this subspace cannot be significantly similar in size to any space with a notably reduced dimension $m, where $m < n$, and we achieve this by demonstrating that the original space's dimension can be significantly reduced while upholding the original dimension increase requirements.

Radiation beam analysis is crucial for achieving maximum potential in utilizing
powerful electron storage rings as part of synchrotron light sources. This paper
presents a method utilizing continuous scans across a fixed detector to gather
data, which is then analyzed to extract key beam parameters. This approach was
successfully implemented at the bending magnet beamline of the National Center
for Nuclear Research's (CYFRON) synchrotron light source, which is powered by a
5 GeV electron storage ring. The beamline in question features a 20 m long
magnet with a 72 meV resolution spectrometer located 17 m from the magnet. A
scan-based analysis method was employed to determine key beam parameters, which
included a central orbit position, horizontal and vertical beam sizes, and a
divergence angle. These parameters were obtained through a combination of scan
data and a central scan position, which was cross-checked by comparing results
obtained using two different analysis methods. This method has the benefit of
obtaining all necessary beam parameters with a single scan setup, which in turn
reduces setup and analysis time. This approach has been made available as an
open-source software package for other researchers to utilize and adapt for
their own beam analysis needs.

This paper investigates a communication optimization problem that is subject to malicious data attacks within a decentralized network. The problem is broken down into smaller sub-problems that are optimized independently by individual nodes, with the results shared with neighboring nodes. Certain nodes then calculate the subgradient of the problem using information from these neighbors, with the goal of minimizing the total communication cost under attack. A distributed optimization algorithm is developed to resist attacks, involving the sharing of quantized gradient information. The algorithm's effectiveness is guaranteed by demonstrating that it converges to an optimal solution under certain conditions, with the added benefit of reducing communication loads through quantization.

The analysis of Cosmic Microwave Background experiments relies heavily on realistic simulations to validate their analysis tools and experiment designs. However, current simulation tools have a limited ability to model the complex instrumental systematic effects that typically enter into the data analysis process in the form of masks, filters, and specific processing steps. As experiments move towards higher sensitivity and smaller features in their data, the accurate simulation of instrumental effects will become increasingly crucial. The simulation tool s4cmb is designed to address this shortcoming by simulating the signal of an experiment in the presence of instrumental systematic effects, including noise models, filtering, and masking, with the goal of facilitating the development of analysis pipelines and validating experiment designs before the data is actually collected.

In this study, we examine how pre-trained language models, specifically BART, solve a fundamental problem - arranging words in order. To understand their approach, we perform a detailed analysis of both synthetic and real-world data using various attention patterns and order-based classification methods. Our findings suggest that BART's success on these tasks primarily relies on its ability to recognize linear dependencies between words and the order in which they appear, rather than more complex, non-linear connections. We also explore the limitations of our approach and potential ways to expand our experiments to shed more light on the topic.

The rapid dissemination of deepfake technology via the internet poses a significant threat to society, prompting an urgent need for effective detection methods. While initially successful, existing detection approaches have begun to falter due to the ease of creating high-quality deepfake media. To address this challenge, this research introduces a novel detection framework called the MD-CSDNetwork, a multi-domain cross-sewn network designed to mitigate the shortcomings of current methods. By integrating a unique combination of cross-sewn attention and anti-symmetric modules, MD-CSDNetwork enhances the ability to identify and reject misleading cues embedded by deepfake creators. The proposed framework has been implemented using convolutional neural networks and achieved impressive results in various configurations, surpassing the current top models on the FaceForeniscs++ benchmark.

This paper proposes a new coding theory framework that assesses the performance of degree-related low-density parity-check (dR-LDPC) codes on a binary erasure channel (BEC). To evaluate the dR-LDPC code performance, the focal point is on the degree pattern, particularly how the degree sequence of a dR-LDPC code affects its error-correction capability. A set of degree-variation measures are introduced to analyze and compare the dR-LDPC code performance. Furthermore, an exhaustive search method is presented to determine the optimal degree sequence for a specific galois domain in search of the maximum degree-variation measure. The results of this research reveal that some dR-LDPC codes with degree sequences of varying degrees outperform the traditional LDPC codes with uniform degree sequences in terms of error-correction performance.

A critical vulnerability in the quantum key distribution system is addressed by randomizing the phase of vacuum states used in its implementation. Although widely applied, this measure is shown to have limitations in the context of the widely-deployed decoy-state QKD system. A detailed analysis reveals that an advanced attack can bypass the system's security by exploiting these randomizations, especially when the degree of randomization is small. A new attack strategy is presented, based on the application of classical-vacuum reference port, which allows for the distinction between real and artificial sources without being detected by the users. This attack results in an increased gain for the attacker, which can compromise the system's security by more than 10^11 factors, rendering it vulnerable to hacking. The findings emphasize the necessity of robust phase randomization in the decoy-state QKD system, particularly by increasing the degree of randomization.

As mobile data traffic continues to escalate, the need for a more adaptable and
efficient communication network becomes increasingly critical. Next Generation
Networks (NGNs) must be highly organized, self-healing, and capable of adapting
to a constantly changing environment. Centralized network management using artificial
intelligence and multi-agent systems can help achieve these requirements, enabling
coordinated decision-making and resource utilization across the network. This would
enable optimal traffic routing, efficient resource allocation, and detection of
anomalies, ultimately leading to faster repair times and a more resilient network.
This article delves into the concepts of decentralized, distributed, and centralized
network management, highlighting their respective advantages and disadvantages.
It also explores the potential applications and benefits of centralized network
management using multi-agent systems, discussing various use cases and presenting
a simulated scenario to illustrate its effectiveness.

In 1911, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he believed could be an intrinsic property of metric spaces. Menger posed two significant problems related to this concept, one focusing on the existence of a topological invariant under isometry, and the other concerning the possibility of embedding metric spaces within higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces while preserving angle functions. This dissertation aims to provide solutions to these problems, initially by establishing the topological invariance of the metric space structure in dimensions two and three, and subsequently by demonstrating that certain metric spaces can be embedded in higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces while preserving their original angle functions.

Let $\mathcal{O}_K$ denote the ring of integers in a number field $K$ and consider a subring $\mathbb{Z}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{O}_K$ with the quotient field $K$. For a given $\mathbb{Z}_0$-module generator $\alpha$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$, we define the rank of $\mathcal{O}_K$ as $\text{rank}_\mathbb{Z}(\mathcal{O}_K) = \text{rank}_\mathbb{Z_0}(\alpha)$. In this paper, we establish upper bounds for $\text{rank}_\mathbb{Z}(\mathcal{O}_K)$ in the case where $\mathbb{Z}_0 = \mathbb{Z}$, specifically for the field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ with a square-free integer $d$ and for Kummer extensions $\mathbb{Q}(e^{2\pi/i p})$. These results are then applied to set an upper limit on the number of linearly independent places on a curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with a specific genus and a particular local ramification behavior.

We present a novel approach to make simultaneous measurements of temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios using a one-dimensional variant of rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy. This method leverages a dual-sensor system, combining time-domain data collected with a picosecond time-correlation technique and frequency-domain data acquired through a supercontinuum-based technique. The time-domain and frequency-domain data are analyzed independently before being combined to yield more accurate results. The time-domain approach determines the pressure and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratio based on rotational decay times and distances between rotational rotation lines, whereas the frequency-domain approach calculates the temperature from a Boltzmann distribution fit. The combined approach shows significant improvement in measurement precision, with an error margin of 0.3 bar for pressure, 0.1 in oxygen-to-nitrogen ratio units, and 10 K for temperature. The precision of this method is largely insensitive to initial conditions and can handle a wide range of gas mixtures. The method also offers real-time measurement capabilities, with a potential for extensive applications in various fields of science and engineering.

The formation of planetary systems relies heavily on the early stages of star formation, specifically the evolution of protostars and their surrounding disks. Observations of gas and solid matter in newly formed stars are compared to theoretical models in this process, using data from a range of facilities, including ALMA, ATLASGAL, and Spitzer. The research focuses on a particular stage of star formation, known as the class 0/I stage, and looks for patterns in planetary systems that form during this period. The analysis reveals a link between the formation of planetary systems and the creation of self-sustaining spiral structures, known as whirls, in protostellar disks. These features can lead to the creation of small solid particles and help to prevent the growth of large planetary bodies by collisional destruction. The study suggests that planetary systems forming in such disks are more likely to have multiple planetary bodies with similar masses, and that these planetary systems typically develop in environments that are not too hot or too cold. The research also indicates that the presence of a binary star system can increase the rate at which whirls are created, and that the mass of the protostar plays a key role in determining the optimal conditions for whirl creation. The study suggests that whirls are more easily created in disks that are moderately thick, and that certain molecular line observations can be used to identify the presence of such structures.
