This research introduces an advanced form of regular expressions, dubbed Extended Regular Expression Inequalities (EREs), which builds on the standard Kleene Star and alternation operators and allows for both inclusion and exclusion relationships between expressions. Both the traditional regular expressions and their infinite variations based on recursive schemes can be represented by EREs. To resolve their patterns, our approach combines the recursive approach with an inequality-resolution technique, enabling efficient handling of complex patterns. The proposed method can be seen as a combination of the Antoniotti and Galliani methods, adapted for the general ERE framework. A basic implementation of the resolution method has been developed using the Nornclato system, a symbolic reasoner designed for string patterns. Nornclato utilizes the Prolog engine, allowing it to leverage the power of Prolog for solving recursion-related problems.

This paper introduces EMA-VIO, a self-navigating visual-inertial odometry system that leverages a single camera and inertial sensor for real-time 6-DoF navigation in complex environments without the aid of external references. To improve performance, we've incorporated an external memory module to store previously encountered environments and adapt to the system's navigation. During network lookup, memory addressing is redefined using a linear cross-entropy calculation to access relevant stored information, enabling the network to focus on previously learned patterns and recall previously navigated routes. Through extensive testing with the VIO-benchmark dataset and real-world applications, EMA-VIO has demonstrated superior navigation accuracy compared to traditional visual-inertial navigation methods and has shown adaptability in recalling previously navigated paths.

We've developed a theoretical framework that utilizes the square-root method for elevated-order effective models of Weyl semimetals. By doing so, we've derived a new set of elevated-order Dirac equations and we've employed this framework to build elevated-order models for both the monopolar and biopolar Weyl points. Our results indicate that this approach can lead to non-trivial higher-order topological phenomena even in zero-dimensional systems. To make this more applicable to real-world scenarios, we've also developed a new method for calculating the elevated-order Weyl Hamiltonian using a square-root technique for the tangent space. Using this method, we've obtained elevated-order Hamiltonian equations for both the monopolar and biopolar Weyl points. Finally, we've used our effective Hamiltonian equations to design and propose new materials featuring zero-energy states protected by symmetry and redressed Berry curvature anomalies.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell's equations, given incomplete and noisy measurements of the electric field. A non-iterative finite element method is employed to solve the reformulated boundary value problem resulting from the quasi-reversibility approach. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through numerical experiments, including results for different boundary data completions and simulations with increasing noise levels.

This paper delves into the vertex operator algebra structure of parafermions, 
based on the $osp(1|2n)$ Lie superalgebra, and outlines the components of 
this algebra. We examine its central extension, primary fields, generating 
fields, and relations with these fields. Our analysis also explores the 
integration of the algebra with the $osp(1|2n)$-module algebra $x^{osp(1|2n)}$, 
discussing their vertex operator algebra structure, primary fields, and relation 
fields.

This paper proposes a federated selective integration approach for matching
neural-based models to share information. When training large-scale datasets
across multiple organizations, there's often a desire to combine models trained
on private data without exchanging information. Our method addresses this issue
by allowing models to selectively share features from their respective datasets
based on model similarities. We applied this method to three classification
experiments and found that federated selective integration yielded better results
than exclusive use of local models and a method that involved integrating all
features from the participating models.

The entorhinal cortex's grid cell network within the brain possesses a unique and intricate neural circuitry. Research suggests that this network's primary element, the grid cell neuron, utilizes a unique firing pattern to help navigate and pinpoint locations within a two-dimensional space. This study aims to investigate various properties of grid cell neurons through a range of firing pattern simulations, utilizing a fire-and-integrate neural system model. Our analysis of these simulations reveals that a wide range of environmental conditions can result in stable, symmetry-based firing patterns, as well as how these patterns adapt to different scales and orientations. Furthermore, our research indicates that grid cell neurons' firing patterns can distinguish between closely adjacent locations, even in a two-dimensional space, and how the neurons' response to movement is influenced by their firing pattern's periodicity and amplitude.

Low-rotating stars with solar-like spectra likely rely on tachocline dynamo mechanisms to generate their magnetic fields. This study examines how a reverse differential rotation in the outer solar layers affects the stability of this process and the resulting magnetic field cycles. It further investigates the potential for magnetic field generation in low-rotating stars with solar-like spectra by altering the shear layer's extent and the Prandtl number in a reverse differential rotation. The findings indicate that a reverse differential rotation in the outer layers stabilizes the dynamo process and causes magnetic field cycles, even at very low rotation rates. It also discovered that a larger than expected shear layer is necessary for instability in reverse differential rotation dynamos, which does not conflict with observations. Additionally, it was found that a high Prandtl number can counteract the destabilizing effects of a reverse differential rotation. It was further found that a reverse differential rotation in the outer solar layers could explain the observed magnetic field cycles in the solar convective zone. It was also discovered that in reverse differential rotation dynamos, the amplitude of magnetic field cycles is inversely proportional to the rotation rate.

The rank expansion problem for elliptic curves over the rationals has been a long-standing challenge in number theory. In this study, we investigate a specific approach, focusing on quartic extensions through quartic fields with Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$. We have developed a method to identify 24-degree polynomials with specified roots, which contain two sets of four conjugate pairs. This allows us to find a quartic field with a desired Galois closure and determine if its discriminant is positive or negative. Leveraging this method, we generated over 3000 elliptic curves with ranks potentially greater than one through quartic extensions in $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic fields and analyzed their analytic ranks via 2-descent. This research includes an examination of the rank expansion conjecture for $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions.

We investigate the thermodynamic properties of holographic systems undergoing from 3D to 2D via a boundary that relaxes, specifically focusing on 2D boundary that contracts and 3D boundary that becomes over-critical. We calculate the quantum equilibrium stress-stress correlator near the edge (QNEC) and derive the corresponding entropy and temperature expressions for both boundaries as they approach a critical point. Notably, we find that the QNEC can distinguish between phases of matter, and we establish a minimum entropy production rate in order for the system to approach equilibrium. We also examine the relationship between the QNEC and another quantity, the bulk stress-stress correlator near the horizon (BNEC), and we demonstrate that they are related by a holographic duality. Furthermore, we explore the connection between the QNEC and another quantity, the Hubble density, and we find that they are correlated, but the correlation does not imply causality.

In the context of the Bloch ball, a key identifiability time $t_{\text{ID}}(\rho, \sigma)$ has been defined to determine, given two quantum states $\rho$ and $\sigma$, how long it takes to distinguish between them. This research focuses on enhancing $t_{\text{ID}}(\rho,\sigma)$ by incorporating a speed limit that takes into account the asymmetry of the states, resulting in a new identifiability time $t_{\text{asym}}(\rho,\sigma)$. It was found that $t_{\text{asym}}(\rho,\sigma) \leq t_{\text{ID}}(\rho,\sigma)$, and the new time can be achieved through a novel strategy using a specific superasmymetric state $\Phi_{t_{\text{asym}}}(\rho,\sigma)$. Notably, $t_{\text{asym}}(\rho,\sigma)$ exhibits monotonicity under any state-dependent channel monotone unitary asymptotic decoupling (MUAD) class $\mathcal{U}(\rho,\sigma)$ that respects the state's geometry, and this monotonicity has a related consequence: it implies that there are distinguishable states $\rho$ and $\sigma$ in the Bloch ball where $t_{\text{ID}}(\rho,\sigma)$ decreases as $\rho$ and $\sigma$ move further apart along a ge
This study proposes a novel estimation for the norm of an interpolation operator established on a function pair, specifically tailored for applications in the theory of splines.

Superconducting quantum circuits are rapidly evolving to become a leading method for detecting coherent states and metrological applications like magnetic field sensing. Real-world usage will require precise control over quantum states, which can be achieved through monitoring and feedback based on resonator readings. Although microwave resonance systems are widely used for this purpose, our study reveals a previously unexplored level of surface loss on the nanoscale, which limits state preparation and needs to be addressed. Utilizing terahertz nanoscopy, we've developed a direct method to measure the microwave radiation emitted from tiny gaps in a resonator, which allows for independent assessment of surface loss, and has shown promising results in reducing loss by adjusting terahertz-vacuum surface impedance. As a result, we've successfully prepared coherent states in a superconducting quantum circuit even in the presence of high surface loss, paving the way for its practical application.

This paper introduces a curve X over the rationals, and establishes curved K-theory functors in a motivic homotopy theory for schemes over X. It also identifies isomorphisms relating curved K-theory functors to motivic cohomology functors, specifically with coefficients in the algebraic K-theory spectrum KGL.

This paper will present a series of processes that contributed to the prolonged development of Venus's atmosphere, leading to the planet's current distinct atmospheric characteristics. Water on Venus played a pivotal role in its atmospheric formation, but the planet's high surface temperature and lack of oxygen led to water being bound to the surface in the form of hydrogen-deficient oxides, thus preventing it from interacting with solar hydrogen. As a result, Venus was unable to utilize its intrinsic water resources to create gases through water vapor cycles, a process that occurs on Earth to regulate CO2 levels. This, in turn, enabled CO2 to persist on Venus, further exacerbated by the planet's inefficiency in retaining hydrogen. The excessive hydrogen on Venus, combined with its high surface temperature and acidic rain, created a self-reinforcing cycle that hindered the release of carbon from the surface. This, along with the inability of hydrogen to break down silicate rocks on Venus, formed a cycle that prevented water from being oxidized, thus preventing further atmospheric gas additions. The prolonged hydrodynamic activity on Venus is attributed to its unique internal heat budget, which resulted from the cooling effects of its thick atmosphere, thus preventing the planet's magnetic field from generating a substantial geodynamo effect. This led to a decrease in Venus's heat loss through hydrogen escape into space, thus prolonging the planet's hydrodynamic activity.

We employed supercontinuum-based reaction nanoscopy to monitor the creation of ions in single sub-micron droplets of glycol, as laser pulses heated the surface, mimicking the effects of solute particles. By analyzing the emitted ions with high spatiotemporal resolution, we studied the formation of clusters on a nanosecond timescale. Our results indicate that solute particles significantly enhance the emergence of ions through cluster formation, as evidenced by reduced ion emission in pure droplets compared to those containing solutes. Furthermore, we observed that cluster formation occurs more efficiently when the droplet is subjected to intense laser pulses than when thermal energy is used, as shown by a greater than tenfold increase in ion emission under laser irradiation. This finding has implications for the generation of cluster ions, as it suggests that solute particles can facilitate this process even in the absence of thermal activation.

This paper proposes a novel method to break down a Matrix Product State into individual unitary circuits in both 1D and 2D scenarios. This decomposition enables a straightforward demonstration of the full controllability of local physical observables in scenarios where direct calculation is impractical due to numerical stability issues. This also highlights the intrinsic relationship between this widely used variational approach and the quantum controllability theory. Moreover, our proposed method provides a practical solution for minimizing the interaction depth of existing quantum simulations, making it an essential tool for this field.

The success of cancer diagnosis and treatment heavily relies on the skills of experienced pathologists who can thoroughly examine histological samples. However, the time and effort required for a detailed analysis of multiple samples can be substantial. To address this challenge, we propose a novel multi-scale network representation for histology images, which combines local tumor tissue patterns and global tissue architecture features. In order to train classification models using this representation, we assembled a large dataset of 12,000 images from whole-slide images of tumor tissues, which were annotated with tumor regions. Our experiments demonstrated that using this representation, a classification model can accurately identify cancerous tissues even when the tumor region annotations are incomplete. Moreover, we observed a significant improvement in classification accuracy when using this representation compared to other network architectures. To facilitate the analysis of whole-slide images, we also developed an efficient prototype system that can accurately identify tumor regions and draw boundaries around them.

Point processes that incorporate multiplicative effects, as seen in the non-linear Hawkes model, have become prominent in analyzing event-based data linked with linear and self-exciting properties. Non-linear connections between events enable the model to capture more complex phenomena, such as sudden increases in event occurrence rates and lasting periods of reduced activity. Despite its advantages, estimating the non-linear Hawkes model parameters is challenging due to the point process's inherent stochastic nature. In this paper, a non-linear Hawkes model is defined and a Bayesian estimation method is developed to obtain accurate results, and the method is tested using synthetic data as well as real Twitter event data. The findings show that the proposed method outperforms traditional methods of the model estimation.

The Rapid Multipole Method employs a particle-system approach to speed up
N-body simulations. This paper addresses concerns over the conservation of
angular momentum observed in previous work, where discrepancies arose due to
the use of approximate interactions in near-neighbor calculations. This issue
is now resolved by introducing a correction to the RMM scheme, involving
the reorientation of particles in their neighborhoods. This change ensures
that the rate of change of angular momentum is accurate, based on exact
positions and motions of particles. As a result, the large-scale structure of
the Universe can be reliably simulated using the modified RMM scheme.

Medical image segmentation models can be limiting due to their reliance on extensive labeled data and potential for overfitting. Semi-supervised approaches can help by utilizing a small labeled dataset in conjunction with a large, though underutilized pool of labeled data present within anatomically similar regions of medical images. However, these regions often contain diverse images with varying anatomical content, necessitating domain adaptation to effectively share information across them. In this paper, we enhance semi-supervised monolithic models with contrastive loss functions to facilitate adaptation, experimenting with models of this type on the task of cardiac multi-structure segmentation in MRI images. Our results show that such modifications are capable of successfully adapting to new domains without prior domain knowledge, outperforming models that don't have this capability by a significant margin of 5.2% in Dice similarity coefficient.

The foundation of contemporary supergravity, often referred to as the '1.5 order trick', has been extensively analyzed. Conducting this analysis in the language of mathematical Lie algebras reveals the underlying issue with the 'trick'. Modifying the algebra to rectify the problem results in a consistent supersymmetry transformation and field multiplet within supergravity. This modified algebra eliminates the redundant 'auxiliary field' component, thereby removing the need to impose constraints on the supergravity multiplet.

Researchers have discovered that magnetized plasmas can differentiate between the left and right circular polarizations of extremely powerful laser beams. This distinction allows for the selective enhancement of one polarization over the other. Within a magnetized plasma, the point at which the laser's polarization alters depends on the strength of the magnetic field. Studies have shown that the stronger the magnetic field, the deeper the point of polarization alteration moves into the plasma. A new study has found that the point of polarization alteration can actually move further into the plasma as the strength of the magnetic field increases beyond a certain threshold, contrary to previous expectations. This phenomenon results in the amplification of the higher polarization over a certain range of plasma depths. Therefore, it is possible to control the amplification of laser beams by altering the magnetic field in the plasma. This means that the high polarization could be amplified, even when the laser is fully absorbed by the plasma, by choosing the right magnetic field strength. This discovery could be useful in creating powerful laser beams from a low-power source, by using a plasma to amplify one polarization over the other.

We have recalculated the electric dipole photon transition amplitude in the tartan lepton model, incorporating the effects of the W boson loop correction. In contrast to a previous study, we utilized the 't Hooft-Low energy effective theory approach, considering the W boson as a heavy field subject to a 1 GeV cutoff. This choice allows us to bypass non-logarithmic corrections. Our results indicate that the W boson loop correction dominates the photon transition amplitude, rendering the photon mass irrelevant. As a consequence, the imaginary part of the transition amplitude is significantly enhanced, with a peak cross-section of approximately 10^-48 cm^2, far exceeding a previous estimate. Additionally, we observed that the photon transition amplitude exhibits a 10^-2 enhancement in its long-wavelength component, primarily due to the influence of the tartan lepton's small mass.

The rank metric, utilized for error correction in linear codes, has been underutilized due to the difficulty of decoding. A proposed decoding approach for symmetric rank errors simplifies the decoding process, albeit with an increased code size requirement. This paper presents an improved decoding method for these specific error patterns, allowing for a reduction in the increased code size necessity. As a result, this new method offers improved performance, especially in scenarios with a high error rate. To validate the improved decoding method, simulations comparing the proposed technique to the original decoding strategy for the GPT code have shown a significant decrease in the rank distance at a corresponding error correction level of nine, occurring at a probability of correction of approximately 0.45.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Fitzgerald:2019qzma}, we obtained two new results:
First, we corrected an inaccuracy in the equation for spinning boundary states BS$_{\Delta,s}$.
Second, we demonstrated that the operator product expansion (OPE) subregion subtractions, introduced in \cite{Fitzgerald:2019qzma}, are equivalent to combining two boundary states, represented by the reflection matrix R and the spinning boundary state BS$_{\Delta,s}$, with specific conformal charges being subtracted.
Furthermore, we found that the reflection matrix R possesses unique properties, causing it to behave as a spinning boundary state with vanishing conformal dimension $\Delta$ and spin $s$.
Lastly, we explored various modes of the chiral CFT$_{2}$ and established that only the chiral stress tensor multiplies the reflection matrix R by a known factor, whereas all other operators produce OPE coefficients along with IR divergent terms.

Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter, $r$, which indicates the ratio of the tensor-to-scalar power ratio and will likely be low, making $r$/$$n_s$ a key target in future experiments. To achieve this, experiments will need to accurately measure a complex parameter that is influenced by several factors, including the primordial power spectrum, which affects how the cosmic microwave background is distorted. In order to remove noise from this measurement, a more sophisticated approach than random noise is needed, which is where a new delensing method comes in. This new method uses a neural network to identify patterns in noise and remove them from the data, which results in an improved measurement of $r$/$$n_s$ even when the primordial power spectrum is not standard. In simulations of the future Simons Observatory, this method results in a 6.5 times better measurement of $r$/$$n_s$ compared to a baseline method that does not remove noise, which could lead to a 50% increase in the probability of the experiment meeting its target for this parameter.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson re-examined and expanded on a previous approach by R. MacPherson (1980) to derive a class formula for Pontrjagin classes using algebraic methods, specifically by linking differential forms to classes in the Milnor $K$-theory. We have conducted a thorough analysis of their method and identified an equivalent differential form for each Pontrjagin class $p_i$, expressible in terms of a closed 2-form $\omega_i$ and a closed 4-form $\tilde{\omega}_i$. Notably, we observed that for $i \geq 2$, the form $\omega_i$ is a multiple of the standard 2-form $\omega_{2,i-2}$, and that the forms $\tilde{\omega}_i$ for $i \geq 3$ can be expressed as a differential of a 3-form $\tilde{\tilde{\omega}}_{i-1}$. Moreover, we found that $\omega_2$ is equal to $\frac{1}{2} \omega_0$, and that $\omega_1$ and $\omega_3$ are both zero.

The Type II supernova 2020jfo exhibited a brief 32-day plateau phase accompanied by a distinct H-alpha profile, which maintained its double-peaked structure throughout 200 days of observation. Initial estimates of the explosion date were confirmed through photometric and spectroscopic analysis, including a redshift calculation of 0.023. Observations of the supernova's early stages and a remarkably stable H-alpha profile over time are presented, along with a discussion of their implications. A comparison of the H-alpha profile to other Type II supernovae showed that it retained a double-peaked shape for an unusually long period. Models of dust temperature and mass also revealed information about the evolution of the supernova's central density and the surrounding dust in the weeks following the explosion.

To significantly boost the counting rate of X-ray monitoring with a Lobster-eye lens, we propose dividing the detector into segments and alternating the transmission of signals from different parts. This would involve using a Lobster-eye lens composed of multiple sub-lenses, with each sub-lens directing a distinct segment of the focal plane. To achieve this, we would use a readout pattern where each sub-lens is activated in succession, with the associated signal being stored in a memory cell before the next sub-lens is activated. This approach would allow for the simultaneous use of multiple sub-lenses, with each one being scanned individually. By utilizing this method with the ChETEC dark matter experiment's Lobster-eye lens, we could potentially increase the counting rate by a factor of 10 to 100.

This paper introduces a novel concept, partial uniform strong ellipticity on a manifold, in relation to a given stage set $\mathcal{S}$. The underlying goal is to extend results dependent on this property, specifically those concerning the existence and uniqueness of smooth potential functions, to the context of semi-continuous functions, particularly those defined in response to a given stage set $\mathcal{S}$. To this end, we first establish an equivalent characterization of the partial uniform strong ellipticity property, followed by an examination of the implications of this property on the structure of potential functions, both smooth and discrete. Building on these findings, we prove that in scenarios where partial uniform strong ellipticity is lost, there exist divergent potential functions, and we further explore the consequences of assuming this property on the structure of level sets. Finally, we demonstrate that partial uniform strong ellipticity is maintainable for stage sets consisting of non-overlapping points and curves.

To investigate how the cosmic velocity field influences dark matter halo mass function, we developed a deep learning-based framework that treats the velocity field as a secondary factor. We trained a deep learning model to predict the probability of finding a halo of a certain mass at a specific location within the cosmic web, given only the mass density field and the velocity field. The model was designed to learn the distribution of halos within the universe without assuming spherical symmetry. By analyzing the halo mass function as predicted by the model, with and without the velocity field included, we found a significant increase in the halo mass function at low mass ranges when the velocity field is considered. This indicates that the velocity field helps explain the formation of smaller halos within the universe.

Music interpretation and song recognition are two goals where audio content is analyzed to derive a representation of the lyrics being sung. In contrast to other applications of music information retrieval, the audio is not a secondary element used in conjunction with a score or lyrics. Instead, the audio is the primary source of information. In this paper, we introduce a data-driven approach to song interpretation employing Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. This method is tested on a semi-supervised dataset containing 1000 seconds of recorded music, resulting in a high accuracy rate of 92.6% among 48 test utterances. A dataset of recorded music with transcriptions is also made available for research purposes.

We have developed a novel numerical approach to create simulations of rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method utilizes an aligned coordinate system and resolves the conservation of angular momentum across the star's surface. We have successfully applied this approach to the simulation of stars in various stages of evolution, from main sequence to compact remnants. Our code has been integrated with the Newtonian code known as the Oslo group's stellar evolution code, enabling an accurate tabulation of structural parameters across the star's evolution. Furthermore, we have established a set of equations governing the conservation of angular momentum, mass, and energy in the simulation, and have developed a suitable cooling prescription for the star. Our code has been made publically available on the GitHub platform.

Large-scale machine learning models have significantly improved in various tasks, yet they still rely on extensive data sets, which are costly to create. A significant shortcoming of existing methods is the manual labeling of key information within visually complex documents, such as forms, invoices, and legal contracts, which are common in business settings. In this work, we automatically annotated over 10,000 documents across 12 categories, a task that would have required over 1,500 days from a single annotator. Our results show that pre-trained document extraction models perform well with minimal fine-tuning, achieving an F1 score of 0.93 on a test set. These models can also generalize to unseen document types with an F1 score of 0.92, demonstrating the ability to generalize across data sets with minimal effort. Our research indicates that machine learning models can efficiently process complex documents with minimal human intervention, reducing labeling expenses to near zero.

The observation of neutron star-black hole (NS-BH) mergers by gravitational wave detectors such as LIGO and Virgo allow for the possibility of detecting gravitational waves through the side channels of electromagnetic radiation. However, the ability to make these predictions depends on accurately training machine learning models on the gravitational wave signals emitted by these events. In this study, a deep learning network was trained to identify and classify gravitational wave signals from NS-BH mergers as well as distinguish between different types of NS-BH binaries. The network was composed of multiple convolutional neural network layers, with the results showing it could effectively distinguish between real and fake signals as well as correctly classify 96% of the binary combinations.

The significant disparity in healthcare outcomes among various socioeconomic populations underscores the necessity to incorporate social determinants of health into the care they receive. However, healthcare providers often struggle to identify which factors are most relevant to their patients, and existing methods lack the precision and comprehensiveness of machine learning tools that can analyze electronic health records. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to automatically extracting SDoH from free-text notes using a marker-driven neural network framework. The framework consists of two components: a machine learning tool to flag potential SDoH within medical records and a rule-based system to filter out irrelevant information identified by the first component. In our study, we utilized a marker-driven neural network to accurately identify a range of SDoH within a dataset composed of over 350,000 medical records, achieving a precision of 94% and a recall of 92%. The results of our research demonstrate the potential for machine learning tools to efficiently extract a comprehensive range of SDoH from large datasets of electronic health records.

This study examines different optimal swimming strategies for a model of the three-part scallop swimmer under varying external fluid resistance conditions. Initially, we consider a simplified model with symmetrical body and flow dynamics, assuming both body and fluid can be divided into distinct components. This is followed by analyses of two asymmetrical body configurations, taking into account the effects of both body and fluid asymmetry. A uniform fluid viscosity model is also assessed. Findings show that asymmetrical body and flow structures can lead to more efficient swimming speeds, and there is a minimum viscosity threshold required for swimming.

The COVID-19 pandemic induced significant changes in human mobility patterns, with the rapid spread of the virus prompting governments worldwide to enforce strict social distancing measures. As a result, people reduced their frequency of leaving home and engaging in outdoor activities, leading to a decline in urban interactions. This study examines how the pandemic's onset affected the way people moved around in eight major US cities and identifies those with significant shifts in behavior under the new pandemic regime. It finds that these individuals with the greatest behavioral changes had a substantially reduced willingness to venture out, in contrast to those with little to no change in behavior, who were more resilient in this regard. Interestingly, the study reveals that the existing disparity in urban interactions was exacerbated by the pandemic, with the gap widening to nearly three times its pre-pandemic level, according to a classification method that quantifies the distribution of urban interactions among different income groups. Furthermore, the study discovers that the increased inequality persisted even after the pandemic, with the reduced urban interactions persisting for an extra two to three months in the lowest income group. This delay in recovery highlights the prolonged challenges faced by low-income individuals in adapting to new external circumstances.

The formation of massive stars is a critical process in the development of massive young stellar objects and the formation of massive protostars. A key aspect of this process is the accumulation of material from the surrounding environment, which can lead to mergers with the protostar. Using a combination of observations and modeling, we investigated the growth of massive protostars by considering the accumulation of material from the surrounding protostellar disk and the possibility of mergers with other protostars. We analyzed a sample of massive protostars located in the core of massive star-forming regions, which are born in pairs or multiples. By comparing the masses of the primary and secondary protostars in these systems, we identified the range of mass ratios that are likely to result in mergers, which could lead to the growth of massive protostars through this process. We also used radiative hydrodynamic simulations to model the growth of massive protostars due to mergers, which could lead to the formation of massive protostars in a short period ($\lesssim$10,000 years). We found that the mergers of two solar mass stars can lead to the formation of a massive protostar with a mass of 20 solar masses in less than 10,000 years, which could have significant implications for the development of massive protostars and the formation of massive stars.

Buchholz and Dollmaier established the concept of local wedge networks in scalar quantum field theory. In this paper, we expand on this idea by introducing wedge-local networks for general Haag-Kastler nets satisfying the wedge-locality property, specifically utilizing the Endomorphisms of Longo-Witten. We demonstrate that such networks satisfy key properties including positivity and symmetry, as well as coherence within each wedge. Furthermore, we establish that for free scalar, fermion, and boson fields, their respective nets align with the described framework.

The rapid development of the fifth generation mobile network poses questions about the environmental impact of its base stations. To address these concerns, we propose a method for calculating the radiation emitted from these towers using readily available data. We apply this method to real-world scenarios, using data from the United States, and estimate the radiation emitted by 5G towers over children, teenagers, schools, and hospitals. We also explore the effects of varying the height of 5G towers and the distance from nearby residences. Our results show that even with a significant increase in the number of 5G towers, the radiation emitted by them is lower than the recommended safety limit set by the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP). We have made our method and data available online, allowing anyone to use them to calculate the radiation emitted by 5G towers in any country.

This research focuses on long-distance, thin-filament deep-water gravity waves with constant vorticity in an incompressible, homogeneous and non-viscous fluid. It aims to extend the Dysthe model, originally applicable to waves without vorticity, to this more complex scenario. A new Hamiltonian Dysthe model is developed to describe the propagation of these waves in both directions along a wall and away from a wall, with an analysis of their Hamiltonian structure. This approach involves a new transformation of the Airy equation, similar to the Dysthe approach, followed by an expansion of the equation and the determination of its Hamiltonian properties. This resulted in a Hamiltonian Dysthe model for the filaments, validated by comparing its coefficients with those obtained from a Dysthe-type transformation of the full water wave equations. This new model demonstrates that a specific relationship between the coefficients of the Dysthe expansion and the water wave equations is necessary to maintain its Hamiltonian structure. This relationship allows for the determination of the dispersion relation of the model, showing that it accurately represents the dispersion relation of the full water wave equations. It also enables the prediction of higher-order Dysthe models and their properties, which can be used to study the propagation of waves with vorticity in other configurations, such as in a channel or in an infinite depth.

This article defines a specific type of differential form over a convex polyhedral surface in Euclidean space and demonstrates the validity of Stokes' theorem for these forms. To establish this result, the article also outlines a method for constructing a particular type of differential form, dubbed the Euler form, in a convex polyhedral surface. The article concludes with an exploration of the Euler form's properties.

Mobile robots operating in dynamic and cluttered environments benefit significantly from sensor fusion and navigation planning systems that can adapt quickly. This study focuses on enhancing a previously developed navigation system for a mobile robot equipped with a sonar sensor in a cluttered environment. The system integrates real-time sonar data with a layer-based representation to create local maps and update navigation paths. Key improvements were made to the system by adjusting its sensitivity to noise from the sonar sensor and optimizing its processing speed. The system's performance was evaluated in a simulated environment and during actual tests using a mobile robot in a library and a parking lot. The results showed that the system was able to maintain a high level of accuracy and adaptability in both environments.

The prevalence of misinformation on social media highlights the need for
effective early-detection methods of fraudulent news. Although textual content
can be utilized for this purpose, the intricate nature of language hinders
conventional approach utilization. In contrast, the simplicity of Character-based
recurrent neural networks makes them an appealing option for sensitive manipulation
avoidance. Integrating a character-based bidirectional LSTM with a classifier
ensemble resulted in outstanding fraudulent news detection performance, with an
impressive 98% accuracy achieved through an innovative use of automatic text
summarization to significantly reduce training data requirements.

This research paper investigates how changing the covariance function of a Gaussian random field affects its characteristics after bending has been taken into consideration. In particular, the study aims to analyze and compare the properties of the field when it is subjected to linear bending and non-linear bending. The paper also explores the implications of this analysis on the development of confidence levels for the field's characteristics under bending conditions.

In a cutting-edge wireless scenario, we explore how a secure power allocation method can be achieved in a Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) system when there is a malicious transmitter present. We present a novel approach to estimate the intended message and anachronistic interference by utilizing a Larmor precession technique, essentially by taking a measurement of the spin precession rate. We then develop a method to calculate the minimum required measurement duration based on the maximum possible duration of message reception. We investigate how the accuracy of our proposed method is affected by the transmission of anachronistic signals, as well as the characteristics of the wireless channel. We also examine the impact of our method's security vulnerabilities and the effectiveness of a corresponding security protocol to mitigate these weaknesses. Finally, we compare the performance of our method to alternative approaches, including a method based on maximum likelihood estimation.

This research introduces an efficient algorithm for computing a specific factorization of a data matrix that minimizes the $\ell_1$-norm, subject to rotational invariance. Specifically, the method finds a factorization of the form $X=US$, where $S$ represents the solution to an L1-regularized least squares problem and $U$ is an orthogonal matrix, such that $S$ is characterized by a minimal number of non-zero components. Unlike prior approaches, the proposed algorithm leverages an accelerated and direct solution strategy for the L1-regularized least squares problem, enabling the use of a highly effective polynomial-time relaxation method for solving $S$. Consequently, the algorithm combines elements of both an iterative shrinkage algorithm and the relaxation method, resulting in a linearly convergent scheme for computing $S$. The method can be applied to large-scale datasets, and its efficacy is demonstrated through extensive numerical experiments.

The rise of BERT-based models in natural language processing has led to enhanced performance in various tasks, including text classification. These models can also be applied to annotate and classify text based on emotions, as seen in the BERT-based studies included in this paper. However, revising annotations made by these models is not well understood, especially in the context of emotion-related questions. This paper aims to investigate the challenges associated with revising annotations made by a BERT-based model, specifically focusing on question texts. It employs a workflow consisting of three-stages: initial annotation, partial unlabeling, and final annotation. The results obtained from 80 participants revealed that the score for inter-annotator agreement was significantly higher during the final annotation stage than during the initial annotation stage. Furthermore, the data collected during the unlabeling stage indicated that the models' predictions often contained inaccuracies. This finding suggests that the BERT-based model frequently made errors, which hindered the revision process. In the analysis stage, it was observed that the annotators' revisions often focused on the underlying causes of the situation described in the question texts, as expressed by the linguistic causal connections. This insight highlights the importance of considering the complex relationships between the situation, its effects, and the underlying reasons that drive those effects, which are essential components of a general theory of emotion.

The concept of order-preserving transformations originates in 1921 with the inquiry of German mathematician Helmut Hasse, who sought to identify functions that maintain the structural order among elements. This historical account reviews the development of order-preserving theories from their early beginnings through recent advancements in the study of minimal first-order theories featuring total order.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, Asynchronous Polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous Polars comprise a unique group of Polars characterized by their orbital periods significantly longer than their spin periods, resulting in unaligned accretion disk and synchrotron radiation. This study aims to differentiate the X-ray hardness properties of Asynchronous and Non-Asynchronous Polars using data from the XMM-Newton observatory, in order to establish a distinguishing feature between these two sub-classes. Our analysis of 13 Asynchronous Polars and 15 Non-Asynchronous Polars during low-count rates revealed a hard X-ray spectrum for both categories, with a distinct cut-off energy that varies between sources. While displaying similar orbital modulation patterns, the X-ray hardness ratios of Asynchronous Polars showed a correlation with their spin periods, with shorter periods associated with harder X-ray spectra. In contrast, Non-Asynchronous Polars exhibited a relationship between their spin periods and the alignment of their accretion disks, with shorter periods linked to more aligned configurations, resulting in harder X-ray spectra due to increased hotspot area. Asynchronous Polars, on the other hand, exhibit magnetic field strengths that are too weak to control the curvature of their high-energy radiation, with potential impacts on their observed X-ray hardness ratios.

This study employs a unified and partitioned Reduced Basis Method (RBM) to tackle Fluid-Structure Interactions (FSIs). The approach involves two methods: unified RBM, which systematizes the reduction process by treating the same type of problem variables as a single entity, and partitioned RBM, which applies the RB method separately to the fluid and solid components. Comparing the two methods shows that the unified approach yields more substantial reductions, especially in the fluid component, due to the similarity of the problems, and this translates to a greater overall benefit. However, the additional computational cost associated with assembling and solving the global matrix in the unified approach may offset these gains, and this depends on the dimension of the problem. A more straightforward implementation is required to match the efficiency of the partitioned method. Nevertheless, the unified approach provides a theoretical framework for addressing multi-physics and multi-domain problems using RBM.

Effective navigation in unfamiliar environments heavily relies on a clear understanding of the surrounding space. To facilitate this, researchers have developed various methods to represent and traverse unknown areas, often utilizing existing mapping techniques such as grid-based systems. These approaches, however, fail to capture the complex layout of many environments due to their oversimplified models. In response, our novel representation framework, HiTMap, has been designed to model the topological structure of an unfamiliar space, enabling efficient navigation using a hierarchical system of sub-environments. To validate our approach, HiTMap was implemented on a mobile robot navigating a complex indoor environment, and the results showed that it can adapt to changing circumstances and recover from errors in its path planning. Furthermore, our analysis of the representation's stability revealed that small disruptions can lead to the emergence of a more stable attractor state, resulting in a new equilibrium, a phenomenon observed in non-linear dynamical systems.

In this paper, we present the system developed by the University of Michigan and Indiana University, which ranked 13th out of 18 participants in the classification of aggressive tweets according to user annotations at the SemEval 2019 Task 6. After conducting a thorough analysis of available data, we decided to train three distinct models using BERT and subsequently applied support vector machine techniques to achieve the desired classification. Ultimately, our approach yielded a micro F-score of 0.2806, exceeding the baseline score of 0.0645.

By utilizing atomic interferometry with atomic spins, it's possible to precisely measure magnetic field alterations down to $10^{-14}$ Tesla in a controlled environment of $10^{-3}$ Gauss. Typically, this method would be limited by atomic interactions with external magnetic fields, but the presence of a superconducting material can significantly reduce these effects, creating an ideal condition for this measurement technique to excel. When a superconducting material is present, it generates a local magnetic field of approximately $10^{-3}$ Gauss opposed to the external field, which can be used to the advantage of the interferometry by adjusting the position of the atomic beam relative to the superconducting material. As a result, it's possible to observe the distinctive 'anti-interference' pattern observed when the atomic beam passes right next to the superconducting material. This achievement could potentially be used to enhance sensitivity in measurements involving atomic spins by using a superconducting material in the form of a thin wire.

In this study, we predict a significant spin-polarized magnetocaloric effect in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides. The unique structure of these materials allows for the creation of a narrow band with high spin-orbit coupling, resulting in extrinsically spin-polarized electrons. A close-packed substrate is shown to induce a specific crystal structure, resulting in a gap opening at the Fermi level along the K-M high-symmetry line in the Brillouin zone. This gap can be controlled through an external electric field, effectively activating and deactivating the magnetocaloric effect. The optimal condition for this phenomenon is identified as occurring at the M point in the Brillouin zone when the FermI level is half-filled, resulting in a large magnetocaloric capacity of approximately 3.1 x 10^4 J/m^3, which is comparable to that of nickel. This phenomenon is further analyzed across various materials in the TMDC family, with the result showing that the optimal magnetocaloric capacity can be modulated through adjustment of the external electric field.

We examine the influence of a nearby metal edge on a 2D electron gas, specifically considering how it affects gap-plasmons within a hollowed-out region. Both a nearby edge with high potential and a distant edge were investigated. In the former case, we found that a high electron density near the edge has a significant impact on plasmon frequency, outweighing the effect of nonlocality. However, when the edge has low potential, we found that both the electron spillover and nonlocality contribute similarly to the frequency shift. In the distant edge scenario, we found that both the electron spillover and nonlocality contribute to the frequency shift, with nonlocality dominating.

Type theory relies on the normalization of types for its core functionality, proving the existence of terms. Normalization enables the computation of unique normal forms, allowing beta and eta reduction to be used for evaluating and proving equality of terms. In the Calculus of Constructions, the types form a CCC (Category Theory with Cartesian Closed Structure) and normalization is necessary for its applications in computer science and mathematics to function properly. However, the formal system needs a robust normalization technique that addresses potential issues caused by the conversion relations affecting the normality of types during reduction. In the Calculus of Constructions, the conversion relations form a cyclic graph that can complicate the normalization process by introducing loops. To resolve this issue, a cut-free resolution-refutation method can be employed to control the reduction process. Normalization can be achieved by treating the non-normalizable terms as control flow statements that redirect the reduction to a specific goal, which can be realized by introducing a special type containing only the base types. This type will serve as the goal for the type of the universe, causing the universe to normalize to it. The presence of the non-normalizable terms will also enable the use of negative translation to extend the type theory with higher-order logic and other mathematical constructs while maintaining normalization. This approach allows the types to retain their normality while incorporating these extensions.

This study delves into the underlying physics of topological quantum phenomena using the one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model as a starting point. We employ both the conventional and modified Hamiltonian approaches to investigate the physics of this model, which serves as a fundamental representation of topological quantum phenomena. Our analysis utilizes the conventional and modified Hamiltonian approaches to examine the physics of this model, which is also a fundamental representation of topological quantum phenomena. Our findings reveal the physical interpretations of the Higgs mode, emergent fermions, and others in the context of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, providing a comprehensive understanding of this model's physics.

This paper examines the underlying structure of a mixture model using probabilistic geometry and Choquet theory, thereby providing a new perspective on the topic. In statistics, mixture models are a versatile tool used to analyze complex data by breaking it down into simpler components. However, interpreting the geometric nature of these models can be challenging due to their inherent complexity. In the field of probabilistic geometry, the Gaussian distribution plays a central role in analyzing geometric structures, particularly in identifying latent dimensions and distinguishing between manifolds. In the context of finite mixture models, the Gaussian distribution can be viewed as a combination of expert opinions, each associated with a specific component of the data. By applying the principles of Choquet theory, the mixture model can be seen as a way to aggregate this information to form a comprehensive understanding of the data. This approach facilitates the identification of underlying structures, such as clusters, and provides a framework for selecting the number of components based on the diversity of expert opinions and their level of agreement. In essence, this paper presents a statistics-geometry-theory framework for analyzing complex data with underlying geometric structures, and highlights the potential for generalizing this approach to other probabilistic models.

Type IIB supergravity is analyzed within the AdS$_5$ x S$^5$ framework, employing a dual description using CFT. The method involves utilizing a CFT dual description to reinterpret supergravity equations derived from the extension of the CFT two-point functions. A previously overlooked supergravity field in the AdS$_5$ x S$^5$ setup is identified using this method, and its associated CFT counterpart is located in the dual CFT description. Further investigation into this new supergravity field reveals its connection to a Higgsed form of dual supergravity previously discussed by T. Hartman, and it is found that this new field causes a decoupling of a set of supergravity equations from the dual loop corrections. The new supergravity field is found to be linked to a component of the bi-linear in the CFT's stress tensor multiplet, and it is shown that its inclusion results in a decoupling of the dual loop corrections to the CFT's two-point functions from the self-interacting supergravity loop corrections.

Developing parallel applications using object-oriented programming techniques is simplified by existing tools, but they often fall short by failing to address memory management issues on GPUs through object allocation methods. To bridge this gap, we present DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator specifically designed for object allocation on GPUs. By minimizing memory waste and reducing conflicts, DynaSOAr outperforms other methods, particularly for large memory allocations, as demonstrated by a benchmark showing a 4x speedup over CUDA's cudaMalloc. The source code of DynaSOAr, a parameterized memory allocator, is also introduced alongside a case study of a GPU-accelerated simulation application utilizing DynaSOAr, which achieves a 2x speedup over CUDA's direct memory allocation.

This paper investigates two types of operators, the sublinear operator T and the bounded operator S, which are applied to functions within the generalized mixed Morrey spaces. A specific condition is established to ensure that T and its commutator [T, S] converge finitely for all applicable functions. Moreover, this study demonstrates that T and [T, S] are continuous on the generalized mixed Morrey spaces, and it also provides a finite bounded norm estimate for [T, S].

A comprehensive theoretical model has been developed to analyze the localized spin states of magnetic adatoms and dimers on a metallic surface. The model is based on an atomic tight-binding representation and takes into account the effects of an external magnetic field through a unitary transformation. Utilizing this transformation, the Hamiltonian is re-expressed in a more manageable form, allowing for the decoupling of surface and bulk components and the redefinition of relevant YSR states. This transformation also facilitates the identification of relevant hopping processes between these states. By applying this theoretical framework to manganese adatoms and dimers on the niobium (110) surface, we are able to interpret recent experimental data obtained via high-field specific heat measurements. These calculations enable us to distinguish between two-dimensional (2D) and quasi-one-dimensional (q1D) YSR states and predict corresponding heat capacity peak patterns. The results of these calculations are consistent with experimental observations, indicating that a single manganese adatom situated in a hollowness on the Nb(110) surface possesses a q1D YSR state, while a manganese dimer positioned in a trench exhibits both q1D and 2D YSR states. Furthermore, we find that placing a manganese dimer within a trench, but closer to its edge, transitions from a 2D YSR state to a q1D YSR state, and that the resulting YSR state patterns are highly sensitive to the spatial distribution of the superconducting pair amplitude.

FourierMask is a novel instance segmentation technique, integrating Fourier series with Implicit Neural Networks (INNs) to create a new approach for instance segmentation, specifically mask generation. INNs have gained popularity recently, offering a fresh perspective on using neural networks for shape representation and generation. However, applying INNs to segment multiple instances relies on assuming that the network can accurately predict unique functions for each instance, given its ID. This assumption is problematic because it's challenging to assess the precision of the predicted shapes. FourierMask addresses these limitations by transforming the implicit function predicted by the INN into a Fourier series, effectively converting it into a explicit form that can be analyzed and compared with ground truth labels through correlation coefficients. This allows for precise matching of predicted shapes to actual instances. FourierMask achieves this by maximizing the correlation coefficient of the predicted Fourier series with ground truth labels instead of working directly with the implicit function. This approach also facilitates seamless extension to multi-class segmentation by modifying the loss function accordingly. FourierMask is evaluated on the MSTAR benchmark dataset, achieving a segmentation accuracy of 85.6% at a 0.5 threshold, outperforming state-of-the-art methods like FourierNet and Mask R-CNN.

Given a closed manifold $M$ and a non-negative integer $k$, we define a confined immersion of degree $k$ as an immersion $\phi: M \to \mathbb{R}^{k+n}$ whose image has a local minimum distance to the origin that is greater than or equal to some epsilon, no matter how small epsilon may be. In this paper, we investigate the range of degree $k$ confined immersions of closed manifolds within $\mathbb{R}^{k+n}$. We first prove that it is possible to fill a sphere of degree $k$ in $\mathbb{R}^{k+n}$, then show that any subset of $\mathbb{R}^{k+n}$ containing a sphere of degree $k$ is not fillable with confined immersions of degree $k$ for $n>1$, and finally demonstrate that all fillable subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{k}$ can be filled with confined immersions of degree $k$.

Analyzing three-dimensional cloud structures is crucial for understanding the behavior of convective clouds and their impact on the Earth's energy balance. While two-dimensional satellite images can provide information about cloud size and shape, they lack information about cloud depth. This research uses data from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and the Multi-angle Imaging SpectroRadiometer (MISR) to create a new method for determining the location of the "veiled core" in opaque convective clouds from space. By comparing the brightness of cloud cores from different viewing angles, this method identifies the angle that best indicates the direction perpendicular to line-of-sight, allowing for the estimation of cloud optical depth and core distance from satellite view. This method was tested using in situ data from aircraft and was found to be accurate within a certain range of cloud conditions. It also showed that the core distance can be as short as one to two times the cloud optical depth, a value that previous models underestimated. This research has implications for improving cloud parameterizations in climate and weather forecasting models.

A new approach is being explored to significantly boost the efficiency of ion thrusters by utilizing a highly intense laser to create a critical mass density threshold in a certain length "d" within a certain time "t". This phenomenon, which we term "translucency time", is essential for ion thrusters as it enables them to operate in a new "self-induced" mode. When a highly charged particle, such as an ion or a relativistic electron, passes through the "translucency time" window, it experiences a strong interaction with the target gas, resulting in the ejection of a large number of ions at a rate that is directly proportional to the "translucency time". This leads to a continuous flow of ions even in vacuum, allowing for the transfer of momentum to a propellant gas through collisions with the ejected ions. This process can be sustained for an extended period by using a train of intense laser pulses, with each pulse creating a "translucency time" window that overlaps with the previous one by a fraction of "d". This overlap results in the creation of a "bubble" of high-density plasma, which acts as a reservoir for the ions that are ejected due to the passage of highly charged particles. This reservoir ensures continuous ion flow even after the "translucency time" window has closed, effectively creating a continuous ion flow source. The NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) has significantly expanded our knowledge of planetary systems with multiple bodies by making thorough observations of the sky. TESS's powerful capabilities have enabled the detection of many new exoplanetary systems and have allowed for a more in-depth examination of existing ones. In this study, a three-planet system, TOI-712, was discovered around the bright K-dwarf TOI-712. By conducting a range of stellar and planetary characterizations, researchers found the host star to be 0.69 solar masses and 0.65 solar radii while the planets had masses between 0.23 and 0.43 Neptune masses and radii between 0.38 and 0.43 Earth radii. The planets in this system, with orbital periods of 19.4, 38.8, and 83.5 days, have egg-shaped paths that increase the likelihood of finding Earth-like planets in this system waiting to be discovered. By modeling the planetary positions and path shapes, researchers were able to confirm the validity of the three-planet model and rule out alternative explanations such as false positives caused by planetary transits in different orbital planes. The study also included a range of follow-up observations, including radial velocity and high-cadence light curves, as well as an analysis of the system's stability, false positives, and the planetary radii.

This study examines the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  Using DFT, we investigated various substitutional and interstitial doping arrangements for both elements.  Carbon was found to have multiple stable configurations, some of which exhibited magnetic properties.  In contrast, nitrogen was found to have a more limited range of arrangements, with some of these displaying magnetic characteristics.  For both elements, the most stable arrangements were found to have a positive formation energy when compared to diamond or N2, respectively.  However, these arrangements can be relevant to the doping process, as they can occur naturally under high-energy conditions.  The distribution of dopant atoms was found to exhibit long-range periodicity, with some arrangements resulting in magnetic properties.  The most stable dopant arrangements were found to have a minimal impact on the Ti and O atoms surrounding them, with some exceptions.  The energy gap of these dopant arrangements was found to vary, with some exhibiting a narrow energy gap that could be useful for them being used in optoelectronic applications. The energy gap of these dopant arrangements was found to vary, with some exhibiting a narrow energy gap that could be useful for them being used in optoelectronic applications.

Although the Standard Model of particle physics remains coherent with current data, the lack of top quark pole mass and broad characteristics such as its form factor continues to be a mystery. Top quark pair production via an invisible elastic channel, $p\,p\to t\bar{t}t\bar{t}$, not considered before, offers a novel approach to investigating the top quark's properties. To facilitate this research, we suggest a new signature with an invariant mass of the top quark pair system above $350\,\text{GeV}$. This signature is characterized by two isolated and opposite-track leptons with the same electric charge, along with missing transverse momentum resulting from the two neutrinos. To improve discovery potential, we examine three different strategies for experimentally measuring the missing transverse momentum and propose three analyses based on the characteristics of the signal and main background processes. The most significant background processes are $p\,p\to t\bar{t}W$ and $p\,t\bar{t}Z$ production as well as $p\,p\to WW/WW$. To estimate the number of expected events, we utilize a Monte Carlo simulation and derive a 95% confidence level (SUSY-13-008) threshold for the cross-section at a 13 TeV Large Hadron Collider with a 25.4 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ data set. This second part of a series investigates the impact of measurement errors on the estimation of turbulence properties within galaxy clusters using radio observations. It was found in the previous study that the statistics of density variations within intra-cluster gas match artificial observations generated with realistic levels of noise. This study proceeds with an assumption that measurement errors are random and constant across all observations. It is demonstrated that even small errors can significantly affect the estimation of structure functions, with their magnitude depending on the spatial scale being examined. At small scales, the influence of errors is more pronounced due to the higher standard deviation of measured values. A method for estimating the accuracy of structure function measurements is proposed, allowing for the reduction of their impact. It is shown that, with this approach, the standard deviation of measured values can be represented as a function of scale and measurement coarray, removing any systematic component. As a result, the ratio of systematic to random variations decreases with smaller scales and shorter measurement spacings. Furthermore, this study provides a framework for evaluating the impact of measurement errors on the recovery of actual turbulence properties, with an emphasis on developing a theoretical model that accounts for the relationship between observed radio observations and their underlying intra-cluster gas.

We investigate the upper richness of infinite graph components under specific Ramsey conditions, examining how the richness of a given graph $G$ impacts the existence of a particular coloring on infinite graphs within it. Our main theorem shows that if every two-coloring of $\omega$ contains a copy of $K^1_2$, then for any graph $G$, the number of monochromatic copies of $G$ in a 2-coloring of $\omega$ is equal to the number of possible subgraphs of size $G$ formed by 2-coloring $\omega$, regardless of the coloring used. We further explore this concept by examining the upper richness of infinite graph components under the assumption that every two-coloring of $\omega$ contains a copy of $K^2_2$, discovering that this condition does not guarantee a certain level of upper richness for all graphs. However, we do find that some graphs do have a certain level of upper richness under this assumption, and we establish a connection between this assumption and another Ramsey theory known as the infinite graph partition theorem.

Located within the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a ring-shaped region filled with molecular gas. Observations suggest that the overall mass distribution within the CMZ is anisotropically arranged, with a greater mass presence along the major axis. To further investigate this phenomenon, researchers have utilized radio astronomy to study the 3.6 mm continuum radiation emitted by dust particles in the CMZ. By analyzing these emissions with the help of the ATLASGAL survey, scientists have mapped the two-dimensional mass distribution within the CMZ. A statistical analysis tool known as the two-dimensional correlation function has been employed to compare the mass distribution within the CMZ to a randomly generated set of star-forming regions. By utilizing this method, researchers have calculated an anisotropic factor that quantifies the degree of alignment between the major axis of the CMZ and the line connecting the Sun to the Galactic Center. With a value of 1.52, this anisotropic factor indicates that the major axis of the CMZ is aligned with the line connecting the Sun to the Galactic Center by a margin of approximately 40 degrees. To validate this finding, a third axis was incorporated into the analysis to examine the relationship between the mass distribution within the CMZ and the line connecting the Sun to the opposite side of the Galaxy. A life-threatening condition called bilateral vocal cord paralysis results from the obstruction of a major blood vessel or tumor compressing the vocal cord nerves, which impairs the movement of the vocal cords and compromises breathing and speech. Its detection through visual analysis of the laryngoscopy procedure is an established method, involving assessment of vocal cord mobility. However, this technique requires significant expertise and is confined to examining static frames rather than the dynamic information present in video recordings of the procedure. In this research, we focus on the analysis of video recordings of a specific moment during the procedure, when the subject swallows, and aim to automate the classification of normal and abnormal vocal cord mobility based on eye and mass center tracking. Our approach uses a feature extraction method combined with a machine learning classifier, and is supported by experimental results using a dataset of video recordings of the procedure.

Our research proposes using qudits of high dimensionality, specifically sQED bases, to simulate quantum electrodynamics in a cavity while controlling the interaction of a charged particle with a single photon. Utilizing the Haar measure, an unbiased method is developed to select random quantum states representing the quantum electrodynamics system, enabling the empirical comparison of quantum states generating classical outcomes similar to those produced by realistic photon detection. Furthermore, our approach allows us to generate superposed qudits and investigate the dynamics of the quantum electrodynamics system using classical outcomes similar to those produced by realistic photon detection combined with sound waves, which include photon decay, interaction with the cavity walls, and a laser field affecting the charged particle.

The interaction between a high-power laser and an electron-positron pair-producing target can lead to the creation of dense positron streams. Analyzing this interaction with the weak field of a laser through the strong field of an electric field from a surface charge, which can occur in thin targets, reveals that polarization of the target can amplify the positron density by a factor of twenty in a specific direction. As a result, the positron density at the peak can increase to ~10^20 cm^-3, and this effect persists even in the quantum electrodynamics saturation regime. Furthermore, due to polarization, the positron angular distribution shifts by approximately 10 degrees in a direction opposite to that expected, and the positron energy spectrum becomes asymmetric, with more energy carried in the polarization direction.

The minimum number of distinct elements in a sequence of lengths, presented in increasing order, that covers all possible distances between elements in a group G is denoted as the group's algebraic diameter. In this study, we establish upper and lower limits for the algebraic diameter of finite groups. Specifically, we prove that the algebraic diameter of any group with a prime power order is four, whereas the ball-and-chain estimate, which is based on the ratio of the group's order to the largest possible value of the square of the lengths between elements, serves as both an upper and lower limit for the algebraic diameter of finite non-Abelian groups. Moreover, we demonstrate that several families of groups, including cyclic, dihedral, dicyclic groups and classical groups, have an algebraic diameter consistent with the ball-and-chain estimate.

A temperature detection IC is proposed that utilizes a thermally sensitive voltage variation in a PMOS transistor to determine temperature. The detector's core circuit consists of a reference voltage generation unit, a temperature detection unit, and a data conversion unit. The reference voltage is produced using a bandgap voltage generator and a voltage divider, and is utilized to convert the temperature-dependent voltage of the PMOS transistor into a digital temperature reading. The detection unit is based on a source follower and a differential amplifier, while the conversion unit employs a SAR ADC that operates at 1.8V and 1 kHz. The detector's functionality is verified through the fabrication of a test chip, which demonstrates a temperature resolution of 0.24°C, an error of 1.4°C, and a conversion energy of 1.06nJ per conversion across a temperature range of -20°C to 100°C.

This study examines the long-term stability of magnetic field configurations in stars, specifically those with symmetrical axes. We determined the criteria for stability by analyzing the interaction between magnetic field oscillations and the stars' internal dynamics. In general, any magnetic field configuration that satisfies the Taylor-Proudman theorem will be stable. However, this stability is compromised when there are ionized fluids present due to the differing rates of shear and buoyancy, which ultimately lead to the magnetic field's breakdown. We developed a set of conditions, based on Cowling's stability theorem, which must be met for a star's magnetic field to be stable. These conditions were applied to various magnetic field configurations found in stars, including those with dipolar, toroidal configurations and those with complex shapes, as reported in previous studies. We found that many stars with magnetic field configurations of this type are likely to have unstable fields, which contradicts previous findings based on local stability analysis.

In this study, we employ quantitative fluid dynamics to solve the functional Renormalization Group (fRG) flow equations in zero-dimensional quantum field theories. Our approach involves analyzing the fRG flow equations as if they describe a dynamic fluid dynamics system and applies a set of well-defined constraints to the system's dynamics. These constraints are designed to mimic the original symmetries present in the underlying quantum field theory. By solving the resulting closed equations, we obtain the RG flow equations for the effective potential in various $O(N)$ model scenarios, including those with higher symmetric representations. This framework can be applied to a broad range of quantum field theories, and it provides an organized and systematic approach to addressing issues of ambiguities in the effective action within the context of fRG flow equations.

Music generation via large language models has seen significant advancements in the last few years. Nonetheless, the ability to generate coherent paragraphs of music remains unexplored within this field. Our proposed model, Pied Piper, builds upon the foundation of T5 and undertakes the task of composing music through a novel meta-inquiry framework. In testing the model's capabilities, we found it to have a clear advantage over a baseline system, even when given the same training data. Furthermore, Pied Piper exhibits a notable capacity for music creativity, as evident in both its training and untrained states.

This work introduces geometric frameworks, a general concept that encompasses both Lie groupoids and smooth stacks. In particular, we define a distinguished class of objects called Deligne-Mumford stacks with separable quasi-hopf algebras, and demonstrate that this category equivalently represents a subcategory of refined presheaves on the category of Lie groupoids. Furthermore, we establish a direct connection between the category of geometric frameworks and a specific subcategory of refined presheaves on the category of Lie groupoids, utilizing the stacks framework.

We investigated the Dragon infrared dark cloud, a region of star formation, to understand the early stages of core development.
